request: Under 21 CFR Part 312 as shown in the supplied eCFR text, when must a sponsor notify FDA of an unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reaction, measured from the sponsor's initial receipt of the information?

A person required to register its establishment under § 807.20 plans to introduce a device that requires premarket notification. Under 21 CFR Part 807 subpart E as in force on 2026-11-21, how long before the proposed introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce must the submission be made?
Under ICH E6(R2), what minimum total membership is recommended for an IRB/IEC, and which two membership characteristics should be included?

A legacy HDE checklist still quotes 4,000 individuals per year as the HUD ceiling. Under 21 CFR Part 814 as in force on 2026-11-21, what prevalence ceiling must the checklist use for the humanitarian use device definition?
Using the CDC Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Tuberculosis page available on 2026-11-21, when must the tuberculin skin test reaction be examined, and who must examine it?
Under 21 CFR Part 814 as in force on 2026-11-21, within how many days after FDA receives a PMA must FDA notify the applicant whether the application has been filed?
A legacy device quality manual still cites ISO 13485:2003. Which exact ISO 13485 edition and edition date does 21 CFR Part 820 incorporate by reference as in force on 2026-11-21?

FDA receives a De Novo request that is accepted without any additional-information submission. Under 21 CFR Part 860 as in force on 2026-11-21, what are the outside time limits for the acceptance notification and for FDA's review and granting or declining order?

A sponsor first learns on day 0 that a case qualifies for ICH E2A's seven-day expedited reporting rule. What is the outer limit for notifying regulatory agencies and, if that full period is used, by what day measured from day 0 must the follow-up report that is as complete as possible be provided?

A sponsor has submitted the initial IND and 17 later submissions, all numbered correctly under 21 CFR Part 312 as shown in the supplied eCFR text. What three-digit serial number must the next submission carry?

A device meets the custom-device meaning in section 520(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. Under 21 CFR Part 807 subpart E as in force on 2026-11-21, must its manufacturer submit a premarket notification at least 90 days before commercial distribution?

A 4-year-old who received BCG vaccine needs TB testing. On the CDC Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Tuberculosis page available on 2026-11-21, does the stated preference for TB blood tests apply to this child?

A primary-care team is rewriting its pathway for identifying and treating primary hypertension in adults, including adults with type 2 diabetes. Which NICE guideline covers that scope, and which earlier NICE hypertension guideline does it say it updates and replaces?

An investigator says that an FDA-regulated clinical investigation may enroll a person without informed consent solely because the research is minimal risk. Under 21 CFR Part 50 as in force on 2026-11-21, is that reason sufficient, and how does the part define minimal risk?

quotes.whole:
(2) Unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reaction reports.  The sponsor must also notify FDA of any unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reaction as soon as possible but in no case later than 7 calendar days after the sponsor's initial receipt of the information.
(3) Reporting format or frequency.  FDA may require a sponsor to submit IND safety reports in a format or at a frequency different than that required under this paragraph. The sponsor may also propose and adopt a different reporting format or frequency if the change is agreed to in advance by the director of the FDA review division that has responsibility for review of the IND.
(4) Investigations of marketed drugs.  A sponsor of a clinical study of a drug marketed or approved in the United States that is conducted under an IND is required to submit IND safety reports for suspected adverse reactions that are observed in the clinical study, at domestic or foreign study sites. The sponsor must also submit safety information from the clinical study as prescribed by the postmarketing safety reporting requirements (e.g., §§ 310.305, 314.80, and 600.80 of this chapter).

quotes.whole:
(d) Followup.
(1) The sponsor must promptly investigate all safety information it receives.
(2) Relevant followup information to an IND safety report must be submitted as soon as the information is available and must be identified as such, i.e., “Followup IND Safety Report.”
(3) If the results of a sponsor's investigation show that an adverse event not initially determined to be reportable under paragraph (c) of this section is so reportable, the sponsor must report such suspected adverse reaction in an IND safety report as soon as possible, but in no case later than 15 calendar days after the determination is made.
(e) Disclaimer.  A safety report or other information submitted by a sponsor under this part (and any release by FDA of that report or information) does not necessarily reflect a conclusion by the sponsor or FDA that the report or information constitutes an admission that the drug caused or contributed to an adverse event. A sponsor need not admit, and may deny, that the report or information submitted by the sponsor constitutes an admission that the drug caused or contributed to an adverse event.
[75 FR 59961, Sept. 29, 2010]

Any findings from epidemiological studies, pooled analyses of multiple studies, or clinical studies (other than those reported under 21 CFR 312.32(c)(1)(i)), whether or not conducted under an IND, and whether or not conducted by the sponsor, that suggest a significant risk in humans exposed to the drug.

Key Terms (21 CFR 312.32(a))
Adverse event means any untoward medical occurrence associated with the use of a drug in humans, whether or not considered drug related.

Reporting Timeframes
Reporting Timeframes
Initial reporting:
For potential serious risks that qualify for reporting under 21 CFR 312.32(c)(1)(i) through (iv): Sponsors must notify FDA and all participating investigators as soon as possible but no later than 15 calendar days after the sponsor’s determination that the information qualifies for reporting. See 21 CFR 312.32(c)(1).
Participating investigators are all investigators to whom the sponsor is providing the drug under its INDs or under any investigator’s IND.
For unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reactions: Sponsors must notify FDA as soon as possible but no later than 7 calendar days after the sponsor’s initial receipt of the information.  See 21 CFR 312.32(c)(2).
Follow-up reporting:
The sponsor must promptly investigate all safety information it receives. See 21 CFR 312.32(d)(1).
Any relevant additional information obtained by the sponsor that pertains to a previously submitted IND safety report must be submitted as a Follow-up IND Safety Report as soon as the information is available. See 21 CFR 312.32(d)(2).

verdict.summary:
DRAFT FOR QUALIFIED CLINICIAN REVIEW ONLY. This document is not medical advice and is not intended for patient care.

1. REGULATORY ANSWER
Under 21 CFR 312.32(c)(2) as shown in the supplied eCFR text, a sponsor must notify the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) of any unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reaction as soon as possible, but in no case later than 7 calendar days after the sponsor's initial receipt of the information (U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Electronic Code of Federal Regulations [eCFR], Title 21, Chapter I, Subchapter D, Part 312, Subpart C, Section 312.32(c)(2); [75 FR 59961, Sept. 29, 2010]; current eCFR version fetched 2026-11-22T23:20:16Z, https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.32).

2. SCOPE: POPULATION, DOSE/EXPOSURE, AND UNITS
- Population: Human subjects/participants exposed to an investigational drug (including clinical trial participants or any other human exposure source, and participants at domestic or foreign study sites in clinical studies of U.S.-marketed drugs conducted under an IND per 21 CFR 312.32(c)(4)).
- Dose or Exposure: Any dose, regimen, or exposure to the investigational drug under an Investigational New Drug (IND) application (or any exposure source from which the sponsor receives safety information regarding the drug under 21 CFR 312.32(c)(1)).
- Units of All Figures: All reporting timeframes in 21 CFR 312.32 are measured in calendar days (specifically 7 calendar days for unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reaction notification to FDA, and 15 calendar days for standard IND safety reports, post-investigation determinations, and FDA requests for additional data). In FDA guidance regarding investigator reporting to sponsors under 21 CFR 312.64(b), FDA anticipates initial SAE reporting will generally not exceed 1 calendar day.

3. OPERATIONAL DETAILS FROM THE SUPPLIED REGULATIONS AND GUIDANCE
- Start of the Clock (Day 0): Under 21 CFR 312.32(c)(2) and FDA's guidance for industry Sponsor Responsibilities—Safety Reporting Requirements and Safety Assessment for IND and Bioavailability/Bioequivalence Studies (https://www.fda.gov/media/150356/download, fetched 2026-11-22T23:20:16Z), Day 0 for a 7-calendar-day report is the day the sponsor initially receives the information for a case that is interpretable as a single case.
- Gating Criteria (21 CFR 312.32(c)(1)(i) & (c)(2)): The event must be a suspected adverse reaction (an adverse event for which there is evidence to suggest a causal relationship between the drug and the adverse event), must be unexpected (not listed in the investigator brochure or not listed at the observed specificity or severity, or inconsistent with risk information in the general investigational plan/current IND if an investigator brochure is unavailable, per FDA's IND Safety Reporting webpage), and must be fatal or life-threatening.
- Notification of Participating Investigators (21 CFR 312.32(c)(1)): Under 21 CFR 312.32(c)(1) and Footnote 22 of FDA's December 2025 guidance Investigator Responsibilities – Safety Reporting for Investigational Drugs and Devices (https://www.fda.gov/media/152530/download, fetched 2026-11-22T23:20:16Z), sponsors must also notify all participating investigators (all investigators at U.S. and non-U.S. sites to whom the sponsor provides the drug under any of its INDs or under any investigator's IND) of all serious and unexpected suspected adverse reactions, including fatal or life-threatening ones, in an IND safety report as soon as possible but no later than 15 calendar days after the sponsor determines the information qualifies for reporting.
- Submission Format and Routing (21 CFR 312.32(c)(1)(v) & (c)(3)): Each notification to FDA must prominently identify its contents as an "IND Safety Report" and be transmitted to the responsible review division in the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER) or the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER). An alternative format or frequency may be required by FDA or adopted by the sponsor if agreed to in advance by the director of the responsible FDA review division (21 CFR 312.32(c)(3)). Electronic submission specifications are governed by FDA's Providing Regulatory Submissions in Electronic Format: IND Safety Reports (April 2024) and FDA Regional Implementation Guide for E2B(R3) Electronic Transmission of Individual Case Safety Reports for Drug and Biological Products (April 2024), as referenced in the supplied FDA guidance.
- Investigation, Follow-Up, and Reclassification (21 CFR 312.32(d)): The sponsor must promptly investigate all safety information it receives (312.32(d)(1)). Relevant follow-up information to a 7-calendar-day or 15-calendar-day IND safety report must be submitted as soon as the information is available and labeled "Followup IND Safety Report" (312.32(d)(2)). If an investigation later reveals that an adverse event not initially deemed reportable is reportable under 312.32(c), the sponsor must submit an IND safety report as soon as possible, but in no case later than 15 calendar days after the determination is made (312.32(d)(3)).
- Additional Data Requests (21 CFR 312.32(c)(1)(v)): Upon FDA request, the sponsor must submit any additional data or information deemed necessary as soon as possible, but in no case later than 15 calendar days after receiving the request.
- Non-Admission Disclaimer (21 CFR 312.32(e)): Submitting a safety report does not necessarily reflect a conclusion by the sponsor or FDA that the drug caused or contributed to the adverse event.

4. FULL CITATIONS OF SUPPLIED SOURCES

U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Electronic Code of Federal Regulations (eCFR), Title 21, Chapter I, Subchapter D, Part 312, Subpart C, Section 312.32 (21 CFR 312.32; [75 FR 59961, Sept. 29, 2010]), current eCFR text fetched 2026-11-22T23:20:16Z (sha256 db41c60ea129): https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-312.32 and https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-312/subpart-C/section-312.32.
2. U.S. Government Publishing Office (GovInfo), Code of Federal Regulations, Title 21, Volume 5, 21 CFR § 312.32 (4-1-25 Edition), fetched 2026-11-22T23:20:16Z (sha256 25450092fab4): https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title21-vol5/pdf/CFR-2025-title21-vol5-sec312-32.pdf.

4. U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Guidance for Industry: Sponsor Responsibilities—Safety Reporting Requirements and Safety Assessment for IND and Bioavailability/Bioequivalence Studies (citing Providing Regulatory Submissions in Electronic Format: IND Safety Reports, April 2024), fetched 2026-11-22T23:20:16Z (sha256 7124849af041): https://www.fda.gov/media/150356/download.

quotes.whole:
§ 807.81 When a premarket notification submission is required.




(a) Except as provided in paragraph (b) of this section, each person who is required to register his establishment pursuant to § 807.20 must submit a premarket notification submission to the Food and Drug Administration at least 90 days before he proposes to begin the introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution of a device intended for human use which meets any of the following criteria:




(1) The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time; that is, the device is not of the same type as, or is not substantially equivalent to, 



(i) a device in commercial distribution before May 28, 1976, or 





(ii) a device introduced for commercial distribution after May 28, 1976, that has subsequently been reclassified into class I or II.








(2) The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time by a person required to register, whether or not the device meets the criteria in paragraph (a)(1) of this section.






(3) The device is one that the person currently has in commercial distribution or is reintroducing into commercial distribution, but that is about to be significantly changed or modified in design, components, method of manufacture, or intended use. The following constitute significant changes or modifications that require a premarket notification:




(i) A change or modification in the device that could significantly affect the safety or effectiveness of the device, e.g., a significant change or modification in design, material, chemical composition, energy source, or manufacturing process.






(ii) A major change or modification in the intended use of the device.










(b) 




(1) A premarket notification under this subpart is not required for a device for which:




(i) A premarket approval application under section 515 of the act, or for which a petition to reclassify under section 513(f)(2) of the act, is pending before the Food and Drug Administration, or






(ii) There is a predetermined change control plan (PCCP) cleared under section 515C of the act, provided that the change is consistent with the PCCP.








(2) The appropriate FDA Center Director may determine that the submission and grant of a written request for an exception or alternative under § 801.128 or § 809.11 of this chapter satisfies the requirement in paragraph (a)(3) of this section.







(c) In addition to complying with the requirements of this part, owners or operators of device establishments that manufacture radiation-emitting electronic products, as defined in § 1000.3 of this chapter, shall comply with the reporting requirements of part 1002 of this chapter.

§ 807.87 Information required in a premarket notification submission.
Each premarket notification submission shall contain the following information:

§ 807.81 When a premarket notification submission is required.




(a) Except as provided in paragraph (b) of this section, each person who is required to register his establishment pursuant to § 807.20 must submit a premarket notification submission to the Food and Drug Administration at least 90 days before he proposes to begin the introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution of a device intended for human use which meets any of the following criteria:




(1) The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time; that is, the device is not of the same type as, or is not substantially equivalent to, 



(i) a device in commercial distribution before May 28, 1976, or 





(ii) a device introduced for commercial distribution after May 28, 1976, that has subsequently been reclassified into class I or II.








(2) The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time by a person required to register, whether or not the device meets the criteria in paragraph (a)(1) of this section.






(3) The device is one that the person currently has in commercial distribution or is reintroducing into commercial distribution, but that is about to be significantly changed or modified in design, components, method of manufacture, or intended use. The following constitute significant changes or modifications that require a premarket notification:




(i) A change or modification in the device that could significantly affect the safety or effectiveness of the device, e.g., a significant change or modification in design, material, chemical composition, energy source, or manufacturing process.






(ii) A major change or modification in the intended use of the device.










(b) 




(1) A premarket notification under this subpart is not required for a device for which:




(i) A premarket approval application under section 515 of the act, or for which a petition to reclassify under section 513(f)(2) of the act, is pending before the Food and Drug Administration, or






(ii) There is a predetermined change control plan (PCCP) cleared under section 515C of the act, provided that the change is consistent with the PCCP.








(2) The appropriate FDA Center Director may determine that the submission and grant of a written request for an exception or alternative under § 801.128 or § 809.11 of this chapter satisfies the requirement in paragraph (a)(3) of this section.







(c) In addition to complying with the requirements of this part, owners or operators of device establishments that manufacture radiation-emitting electronic products, as defined in § 1000.3 of this chapter, shall comply with the reporting requirements of part 1002 of this chapter.

(2) The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time by a person required to register, whether or not the device meets the criteria in paragraph (a)(1) of this section.

        
(3) The device is one that the person currently has in commercial distribution or is reintroducing into commercial distribution, but that is about to be significantly changed or modified in design, components, method of manufacture, or intended use. The following constitute significant changes or modifications that require a premarket notification:

        
(i) A change or modification in the device that could significantly affect the safety or effectiveness of the device, e.g., a significant change or modification in design, material, chemical composition, energy source, or manufacturing process.

        
(ii) A major change or modification in the intended use of the device.

            (ii) There is a predetermined change control plan (PCCP) cleared under section 515C of the act, provided that the change is consistent with the PCCP.

verdict.summary:
DRAFT FOR QUALIFIED CLINICIAN AND REGULATORY REVIEW — NOT MEDICAL ADVICE AND NOT FOR PATIENT CARE.

### Regulatory Determination: Premarket Notification (510(k)) Submission Lead Time

**Required Submission Lead Time:** **At least 90 days** before the proposed introduction or delivery for introduction of the device into interstate commerce for commercial distribution.

---

### Governing Regulation and Edition Verification
- **Primary Provision:** 21 CFR Part 807, Subpart E, § 807.81(a) (*When a premarket notification submission is required*), 42 FR 42526 (Aug. 23, 1977), as amended at 72 FR 73601 (Dec. 28, 2007) and 89 FR 18792 (Mar. 15, 2024).
- **Version / In-Force Status on 2026-11-21:** Confirmed against the electronic Code of Federal Regulations (eCFR) current text of 21 CFR § 807.81 fetched on 2026-11-22T23:23:35Z (URL: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-H/part-807/subpart-E/section-807.81), the Daily eCFR edition dated 2026-11-12 (https://ecfr.io/Title-21/Part-807/Subpart-E), and the 2025 annual CFR edition (`CFR-2025-title21-vol8-sec807-81.xml`, edition date 2025-04-01). No amendments occurred between March 15, 2024 and November 22, 2026; therefore, the text below reflects the exact regulation in force on 2026-11-21.

---

### Regulatory Scope, Population, and Timing Rule
1. **Regulated Entity and Target Population/Device Scope:** Under 21 CFR § 807.81(a), the requirement applies to each person required to register an establishment pursuant to 21 CFR § 807.20 who proposes to begin the introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution of a **medical device intended for human use** (no clinical dosing or therapeutic exposure applies; this is a premarket regulatory filing requirement) when any of the following criteria in § 807.81(a)(1)–(3) are met:
   - **First-time commercial distribution of a new device type (§ 807.81(a)(1)):** The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time and is not of the same type as, or not substantially equivalent to, (i) a device in commercial distribution before May 28, 1976, or (ii) a device introduced after May 28, 1976 that was subsequently reclassified into Class I or Class II.
   - **First-time commercial distribution by that registrant (§ 807.81(a)(2)):** The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time by a person required to register under § 807.20, regardless of whether § 807.81(a)(1) applies.
   - **Significant change or modification (§ 807.81(a)(3)):** The device is currently in commercial distribution or is being reintroduced, and is about to be significantly changed or modified in design, components, method of manufacture, or intended use (specifically: (i) a change/modification that could significantly affect safety or effectiveness, such as design, material, chemical composition, energy source, or manufacturing process; or (ii) a major change/modification in intended use).

2. **Mandatory Minimum Lead Time:** Except as provided in 21 CFR § 807.81(b), the premarket notification submission (containing the information specified in 21 CFR § 807.87) must be submitted to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) **at least 90 days** (unit: calendar days) before the proposed introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution (21 CFR § 807.81(a)).

3. **Statutory/Regulatory Exceptions and Related Deadlines Noted in Subpart E:**
   - **Exceptions under 21 CFR § 807.81(b)(1):** A premarket notification under Subpart E is not required for a device for which (i) a premarket approval application (PMA) under section 515 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) or a reclassification petition under section 513(f)(2) of the FD&C Act is pending before FDA, or (ii) a predetermined change control plan (PCCP) has been cleared under section 515C of the FD&C Act, provided the change is consistent with that PCCP.
   - **Labeling exception/alternative under 21 CFR § 807.81(b)(2):** For significant modifications under § 807.81(a)(3), the appropriate FDA Center Director may determine that the submission and grant of a written request for an exception or alternative under 21 CFR § 801.128 or § 809.11 satisfies § 807.81(a)(3).
   - **Custom devices (21 CFR § 807.85(a)):** Custom devices within the meaning of section 520(b) of the FD&C Act are exempt from premarket notification requirements under Subpart E.
   - **Radiation-emitting electronic products (21 CFR § 807.81(c)):** Owners or operators of device establishments manufacturing radiation-emitting electronic products (as defined in 21 CFR § 1000.3) must also comply with reporting requirements in 21 CFR Part 1002.
   - **Additional information / resubmission timing (21 CFR Part 807, Subpart E):** If FDA issues a written request for additional information because the original submission lacks sufficient data, the submitter may either submit the requested data or submit a new premarket notification at least **90 days** (unit: days) before intending to market the device (or submit a PMA under section 515); failure to submit additional information within **30 days** (unit: days) of the request results in the submission being considered withdrawn. Separately, under 21 CFR § 807.95(b), where statutory confidentiality conditions apply, FDA will not publicly disclose the existence of a submission for **90 days** (unit: days) from receipt (or **90 days** after receipt of a complete submission following a § 807.87(h) request), and will make a 510(k) summary publicly available within **30 days** (unit: days) after issuing a substantial equivalence determination.

4. **Operational Note:** Submitting at least 90 days prior to proposed commercial distribution satisfies the regulatory filing lead-time mandate in 21 CFR § 807.81(a), which is distinct from FDA's substantive review and clearance determination; the device may not be marketed until FDA issues an order of substantial equivalence or other applicable marketing authorization.

Each premarket notification submission shall contain the following information:
(a) The device name, including both the trade or proprietary name and the common or usual name or classification name of the device.
(b) The establishment registration number, if applicable, of the owner or operator submitting the premarket notification submission.
(c) The class in which the device has been put under section 513 of the act and, if known, its appropriate panel;

Each premarket notification submission shall contain the following information:

Which was introduced or delivered for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution before December 1, 1990; and
§ 807.93 Content and format of a 510(k) statement.
§ 807.94 Format of a class III certification.

The Commissioner requests in writing additional information regarding the device pursuant to § 807.87(h), in which case the Commissioner will not disclose the existence of the submission until 90 days after the Food and Drug Administration's receipt of a complete premarket notification submission;

The Commissioner determines that the device intended to be introduced is a class III device and cannot be marketed without premarket approval or reclassification, in which case the Commissioner will not disclose the existence of the submission unless a petition for reclassification is submitted under section 513(f)(2) of the act and its existence can be disclosed under § 860.5(d) of this chapter; or

FDA will make a 510(k) summary of the safety and effectiveness data available to the public within 30 days of the issuance of a determination that the device is substantially equivalent to another device. Accordingly, even when a 510(k) submitter has complied with the conditions set forth in paragraphs (b) and (c) of this section, confidentiality for a premarket notification submission cannot be granted beyond 30 days after FDA issues a determination of equivalency.

quotes.whole: 2.12.10 When using computerised systems in a clinical trial, the investigator/institution should do the following: (a) For systems deployed by the investigator/institution, ensure that appropriate individuals have secure and attributable access; (b) For systems deployed by the sponsor, notify the sponsor when access permissions need to be changed or revoked from an individual; (c) For systems deployed by the investigator/institution specifically for the purposes of clinical trials, ensure that the requirements for computerised systems in section 4 are addressed proportionate to the risks to participants and to the importance of the data; (d) Where equipment for data acquisition is provided to trial participants by the investigator, ensure that traceability is maintained and that participants are provided with appropriate training; (e) Ensure that incidents in the use and operation of computerised systems, which in the investigator’s/institution’s judgement may have a significant and/or persistent impact on the trial data or system security, are reported to the sponsor and, where applicable, to the IRB/IEC.

Regulatory Deliverable: IRB/IEC Minimum Membership and Required Composition Characteristics Under ICH E6(R2)

1. Scope, Applicable Population, and Exposure Context
- Governing Guideline: International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use (ICH) Guideline for Good Clinical Practice E6(R2) — Integrated Addendum to ICH E6(R1) (Step 4 adopted November 2016; EMA/CHMP/ICH/135/1995 Step 5 Revision 2; FDA Guidance for Industry).
- Applicable Population: Human subjects involved in clinical trials whose rights, safety, and well-being are protected by an Institutional Review Board (IRB) or Independent Ethics Committee (IEC) (ICH E6(R2), Glossary: Definition of IRB/IEC).
- Dose or Exposure: Not applicable (regulatory committee governance and composition standard rather than a therapeutic intervention).

2. Direct Answers (ICH E6(R2), Section 3.2.1)
Under ICH E6(R2), Section 3.2.1 ('Composition, Functions, and Operations'), the guideline states verbatim:
"3.2.1 The IRB/IEC should consist of a reasonable number of members, who collectively have the qualifications and experience to review and evaluate the science, medical aspects, and ethics of the proposed trial. It is recommended that the IRB/IEC should include:
(a) At least five members.
(b) At least one member whose primary area of interest is in a nonscientific area.
(c) At least one member who is independent of the institution/trial site.
Only those IRB/IEC members who are independent of the investigator and the sponsor of the trial should vote/provide opinion on a trial-related matter.
A list of IRB/IEC members and their qualifications should be maintained."

Accordingly:
- Recommended Minimum Total Membership: 5 members (specifically, "[a]t least five members"; ICH E6(R2), Section 3.2.1(a)).
- Two Membership Characteristics That Should Be Included:
  1. Nonscientific representation: At least 1 member ("[a]t least one member") whose primary area of interest is in a nonscientific area (ICH E6(R2), Section 3.2.1(b)).
  2. Institutional/site independence: At least 1 member ("[a]t least one member") who is independent of the institution/trial site (ICH E6(R2), Section 3.2.1(c)).

3. Complementary Composition, Voting, and Jurisdictional Considerations
- Recommendation vs. Binding Mandate: ICH E6(R2) Section 3.2.1 frames the 5-member floor and the two specific member characteristics using recommendation language ("It is recommended that the IRB/IEC should include..."), while also stating in Section 3.2.2 that the IRB/IEC "should comply with GCP and with the applicable regulatory requirement(s)." Similarly, the ICH E6(R2) Glossary notes that the legal status, composition, function, operations, and regulatory requirements pertaining to IECs may differ among countries, provided the committee acts in agreement with GCP. Reviewing clinicians and regulatory leads must therefore verify applicable national/local regulations (for example, national statutory minimums or quorum rules) in the trial's jurisdiction.
- Collective Qualification and Quorum: Regardless of headcount above the 5-member recommended minimum, the members must collectively possess the qualifications and experience to evaluate the science, medical aspects, and ethics of the proposed trial (ICH E6(R2), Section 3.2.1). Decisions must be made at announced meetings with at least a quorum present as stipulated in the IRB/IEC's written operating procedures (ICH E6(R2), Section 3.2.3), and the IRB/IEC must document its composition (names and qualifications of members) and establishing authority in written procedures (ICH E6(R2), Sections 3.2.1 and 3.3.1).
- Voting and Deliberation Independence: Only IRB/IEC members who are independent of the investigator and the sponsor of the trial should vote or provide an opinion on a trial-related matter (ICH E6(R2), Section 3.2.1), and only members who participate in the IRB/IEC review and discussion should vote/provide opinion and/or advice (ICH E6(R2), Section 3.2.4). While the investigator may provide information on any aspect of the trial, the investigator should not participate in IRB/IEC deliberations or voting (ICH E6(R2), Section 3.2.5). Nonmembers with expertise in special areas may be invited for assistance (ICH E6(R2), Section 3.2.6).
- Version Note (ICH E6(R3) Continuity): For reference only (outside the ICH E6(R2) constraint of this request), the subsequent ICH E6(R3) Step 4 Final Consolidated Guideline (Section 1.3.1) retains the recommendation of at least 5 members and at least 1 independent member, while updating the nonscientific characteristic wording from "nonscientific area" to "not in medical sciences."

4. Full Citations
- European Medicines Agency (EMA). ICH Guideline for Good Clinical Practice E6(R2), Step 5 Revision 2 (EMA/CHMP/ICH/135/1995), Section 3.2.1–3.2.6, Section 3.3.1, and Glossary. https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/scientific-guideline/ich-guideline-good-clinical-practice-e6r2-step-5-revision-2_en.pdf
- U.S. Department of Health and Human Services / Food and Drug Administration (FDA). E6(R2) Good Clinical Practice: Integrated Addendum to ICH E6(R1) — Guidance for Industry, Section 3.2.1–3.2.6, Section 3.3.1, and Glossary. https://www.hhs.gov/guidance/sites/default/files/hhs-guidance-documents/FDA/E6(R2)-Good-Clinical-Practice_-Integrated-Addendum-to-ICH-E6(R1)-_-Guidance-for-Industry.pdf

- International Council for Harmonisation (ICH). findings.question:
1. A legacy HDE checklist still quotes 4,000 individuals per year as the HUD ceiling. Under 21 CFR Part 814 as in force on 2026-11-21, what prevalence ceiling must the checklist use for the humanitarian use device definition?
2. Whether the checklist's intended regulatory baseline is the current 21 CFR Part 814 (ceiling of 8,000 individuals per year per the amended § 814.100(a)(2)) — assuming this, when a different baseline or interpretation is intended, would change the answer.

quotes.whole:
§ 814.100 Purpose and scope.




(a) This subpart H implements sections 515A and 520(m) of the act.






(b) The purpose of section 520(m) is, to the extent consistent with the protection of the public health and safety and with ethical standards, to encourage the discovery and use of devices intended to benefit patients in the treatment or diagnosis of diseases or conditions that affect or are manifested in not more than 8,000 individuals in the United States per year. This subpart provides procedures for obtaining:




(1) HUD designation of a medical device; and






(2) Marketing approval for the HUD notwithstanding the absence of reasonable assurance of effectiveness that would otherwise be required under sections 514 and 515 of the act.








(c) Section 515A of the act is intended to ensure the submission of readily available information concerning:




(1) Any pediatric subpopulations (neonates, infants, children, adolescents) that suffer from the disease or condition that the device is intended to treat, diagnose, or cure; and






(2) The number of affected pediatric patients.








(d) Although a HUD may also have uses that differ from the humanitarian use, applicants seeking approval of any non-HUD use shall submit a PMA as required under § 814.20, or a premarket notification as required under part 807 of this chapter.






(e) Obtaining marketing approval for a HUD involves two steps:




(1) Obtaining designation of the device as a HUD from FDA's Office of Orphan Products Development, and






(2) Submitting an HDE to the Office of Product Evaluation and Quality (OPEQ), Center for Devices and Radiological Health (CDRH), the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER), or the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER), as applicable.








(f) A person granted an exemption under section 520(m) of the act shall submit periodic reports as described in § 814.126(b).





(g) FDA may suspend or withdraw approval of an HDE after providing notice and an opportunity for an informal hearing.

Humanitarian Use Device Designations Guidance
On December 13, 2016, Section 3052 of the 21st Century Cures Act (Pub. L. No. 114-255) changed the population estimate required to qualify for Humanitarian Use Device (HUD) designation from "fewer than 4,000" to "not more than 8,000." Accordingly, a HUD is now defined as a medical device intended to benefit patients in the treatment or diagnosis of a disease or condition that affects or is manifested in not more than 8,000 individuals in the United States per year. The full text of the 21st Century Cures Act is available at:https://www.congress.gov/114/bills/hr34/BILLS-114hr34eah.pdf.

quotes.whole:
The Humanitarian Use Device or HUD program was established in 1990 with passage of the Safe Medical Devices Act and creates an alternative pathway for getting market approval for medical devices that may help people with rare diseases or conditions. As defined by 21 CFR 814.3(n), and updated by the 21st Century Cures Act, a HUD is a “medical device intended to benefit patients in the treatment or diagnosis of a disease or condition that affects or is manifested in not more than 8,000 individuals in the United States per year.” In order to obtain HUD designation, the applicant must provide documentation, with appended authoritative references, to demonstrate that the device meets this definition.
In addition to the documentation describing the disease or condition, the applicant must also provide the proposed indications for use of the device, and the reasons why such a device is needed for the patient population. One aspect that has become increasingly difficult is if the HUD is proposed for an indication that represents a subset of a common disease or condition. In these situations, the applicant must demonstrate that the subset is an “orphan subset.”

quotes.whole:
An “orphan subset” is a regulatory phrase used to describe the subset of individuals with a non-rare disease or condition on whom use of a device is appropriate, where use of the device on the remaining individuals with that disease or condition would be inappropriate given some intrinsic feature of the device (e.g., adverse event profile or mode of action). An “orphan subset” is not a readily identifiable subset or a group of patients who meet or do not meet the inclusion and exclusion criteria for a clinical study. Likewise, they are not patients with an unmet medical need. If the HUD application is designated, the applicant can then submit the HDE marketing application to the Center for Devices and Radiological Health (CDRH) or Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER) for marketing review.

Purpose and scope.

(2) The number of affected pediatric patients.

verdict.summary:
DRAFT FOR QUALIFIED CLINICIAN AND REGULATORY REVIEW ONLY. This document is not medical advice and is not for patient care.

1. REGULATORY DETERMINATION
Under 21 CFR Part 814 as in force on 2026-11-21, the legacy HDE checklist must replace the obsolete ceiling of 4,000 individuals per year with a prevalence ceiling of not more than 8,000 (<= 8,000) individuals in the United States per year (21 CFR § 814.3(n); 21 CFR § 814.100(b), eCFR current as of 2026-11-22T23:30:01Z; 2025 CFR Title 21, Vol. 8, Part 814).

2. STATUTORY AND REGULATORY BASIS (WITH VERSION CITATIONS)
- Definition of HUD (21 CFR § 814.3(n), eCFR Title 21, Part 814, fetched 2026-11-22T23:30:01Z): "HUD (humanitarian use device) means a medical device intended to benefit patients in the treatment or diagnosis of a disease or condition that affects or is manifested in not more than 8,000 individuals in the United States per year."
- Purpose and Scope of Subpart H (21 CFR § 814.100(b), 61 FR 33244, June 26, 1996, as amended through 82 FR 26349, June 7, 2017, and 85 FR 18442, Apr. 2, 2020; eCFR fetched 2026-11-22T23:30:01Z): Implements sections 515A and 520(m) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to encourage discovery and use of devices intended to benefit patients in the treatment or diagnosis of diseases or conditions that affect or are manifested in not more than 8,000 individuals in the United States per year.
- Statutory Amendment (Section 3052, 21st Century Cures Act, Pub. L. No. 114-255, Dec. 13, 2016; FDA Humanitarian Use Device (HUD) Designation Program, accessed 2026-11-22T23:30:01Z): Raised the HUD qualifying population estimate from "fewer than 4,000" to "not more than 8,000" individuals in the United States per year (codified in 21 CFR Part 814 via 82 FR 26349, June 7, 2017).
- Correction to Project Assumptions: Note that the exact regulatory boundary is "not more than 8,000" (inclusive, <= 8,000 individuals in the United States per year), rather than "fewer than 8,000," and the governing HUD definition citations are 21 CFR § 814.3(n) and § 814.100(b) (alongside § 814.102(a)(5)), rather than § 814.100(a)(2).

3. READY-TO-APPLY HDE CHECKLIST UPDATE TEXT
Replace any checklist item quoting "4,000" or "fewer than 4,000" with the following updated items:

- Checklist Item A — HUD Population Prevalence Ceiling (Treatment or Diagnosis):
  "Verify that the medical device is intended to benefit patients in the treatment or diagnosis of a disease or condition that affects or is manifested in not more than 8,000 (<= 8,000) individuals in the United States per year, supported by appended authoritative references (e.g., specialized medical journal citations, textbooks, specialized medical society proceedings, governmental statistics publications, or credible research/survey conclusions if literature does not exist)." [Source: 21 CFR § 814.3(n), § 814.100(b), § 814.102(a)(5), eCFR current as of 2026-11-21]

- Checklist Item B — Additional Diagnostic Device Exposure Ceiling:
  "If the device is intended for diagnostic purposes, verify documentation demonstrating that not more than 8,000 (<= 8,000) patients in the United States per year would be subjected to diagnosis using the device (device exposure ceiling)." [Source: 21 CFR § 814.102(a)(5), § 814.102(b)(3)(ii), eCFR current as of 2026-11-21]

- Checklist Item C — Medically Plausible Subset (Orphan Subset) Criterion:
  "If the proposed indication represents a subset of a non-rare/common disease or condition, verify documentation demonstrating that the defined patient population is a medically plausible subset ('orphan subset') based on an intrinsic feature of the device (e.g., adverse event profile or mode of action) making use inappropriate in the remaining population, rather than clinical study inclusion/exclusion criteria or unmet need alone." [Source: 21 CFR § 814.102(a)(3), § 814.102(b)(3)(iii); FDA HUD Designation Program, accessed 2026-11-22]

- Checklist Item D — Post-Approval Periodic Reporting Threshold (Related Threshold Check):
  "For post-approval HDE periodic reports, verify tracking of the number of devices shipped or sold since initial marketing approval; if the number shipped or sold exceeds 8,000 devices, verify inclusion of an explanation and estimate of the number of devices used per patient (and, if a single device is used on multiple patients, an estimate of the number of patients treated or diagnosed with the device and the basis for the estimate)." [Source: 21 CFR § 814.126(b)(1)(iii), eCFR current as of 2026-11-21]

4. POPULATION COUNTING AND UNITS CLARIFICATION
- Population: Individuals in the United States (all ages, with pediatric subpopulations—neonates, infants, children, adolescents, defined as 21 years of age or younger at diagnosis or treatment under 21 CFR § 814.3(s)—separately documented under 21 CFR § 814.100(c)).
- Metric and Units: Annual U.S. disease/condition prevalence ("not more than 8,000 individuals in the United States per year"), not total devices sold. For diagnostic devices specifically, both disease prevalence (<= 8,000 individuals in the United States per year) and annual U.S. diagnostic exposure (<= 8,000 patients in the United States subjected to diagnosis by the device per year) must be satisfied (21 CFR § 814.102(a)(5), § 814.102(b)(3)(i)–(ii)).

5. REFERENCES
1. 21 CFR Part 814 (specifically §§ 814.3(m)–(n), (s), 814.100, 814.102, 814.126), Electronic Code of Federal Regulations (eCFR), Title 21, Chapter I, Subchapter H, as in force on 2026-11-21 (fetched 2026-11-22T23:30:01Z from https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-814.3 and https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-H/part-814/subpart-H).
2. 21 CFR Part 814, Code of Federal Regulations, 2025 Edition, Title 21, Vol. 8 (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title21-vol8/xml/CFR-2025-title21-vol8-part814.xml, fetched 2026-11-22T23:30:01Z).
3. 21st Century Cures Act, Pub. L. No. 114-255, Section 3052 (enacted Dec. 13, 2016); implemented in 21 CFR Part 814 at 82 FR 26349 (June 7, 2017).
4. U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), "Humanitarian Use Device (HUD) Designation Program" (https://www.fda.gov/industry/medical-products-rare-diseases-and-conditions/humanitarian-use-device-hud-designation-program, fetched 2026-11-22T23:30:01Z).

After 48–72 hours, the skin test reaction must be examined by a trained health care worker. The health care worker measures any swelling where the tuberculin was injected to determine if the reaction to the test is positive or negative.
TB skin tests are an acceptable alternative in situations where a TB blood test is not available, is too costly, or is too burdensome.

Interpreting TB blood test results
Interpretation of TB blood test results depends on the test being used.
QFT-Plus results are based on the amount of IFN-γ that is released in response to the antigens and to the control substances after the blood has been incubated these substances.

Laboratories should provide both the qualitative and quantitative results.
For qualitative results
QFT-Plus results are reported as positive, negative, or indeterminate.
T-Spot results are reported as positive, borderline, negative, or invalid.
Quantitative results are reported as numerical values that include responses to the TB antigen and two controls, nil and mitogen.
Specific guidance is not available for interpreting quantitative IGRA results.
These results may be helpful for understanding qualitative results in individual cases, in combination with risk factors.
Interpreting TB skin test results
Interpretation of TB skin test reactions depends on the measurement of induration (firm swelling) in millimeters (mm) across the arm, the person’s risk of acquiring TB infection, and the risk of progression to disease if infected.  For more details on interpreting TB skin test results, please visit Clinical Testing Guidance for Tuberculosis: Tuberculin Skin Test.
TB skin results should only be read by a trained health care professional. Consult with your state and local public health authorities to determine who is authorized to place and read TB skin tests in your state.

quotes.whole:
Tuberculin Skin Testing
What is it?
The Mantoux tuberculin skin test (TST) is one method
of determining whether a person is infected with
Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Reliable administration
and reading of the TST requires standardization of
procedures, training, supervision, and practice.
How is the TST Administered?
The TST is performed by injecting 0.1 ml of tuberculin
purified protein derivative (PPD) into the inner surface
of the forearm. The injection should be made with a
tuberculin syringe, with the needle bevel facing upward.
The TST is an intradermal injection. When placed
correctly, the injection should produce a pale elevation of
the skin (a wheal) 6 to 10 mm in diameter.
How is the TST Read?
The skin test reaction should be read between 48 and 72
hours after administration by a health care worker trained
to read TST results. A patient who does not return within
72 hours will need to be rescheduled for another skin test.
The reaction should be measured in millimeters of the
induration (firm swelling). The reader should not measure
erythema (redness). The diameter of the indurated area
should be measured across the forearm (perpendicular to
the long axis).

What is a Boosted Reaction?
A boosted reaction occurs mainly in previously infected,
older adults whose ability to react to tuberculin has
decreased over time. When given a TST years after
infection, these persons may have an initial negative
reaction. However, the TST may stimulate the immune
system, causing a positive or boosted reaction to
subsequent tests. Giving a second TST after an initial
negative TST reaction is called two-step testing.

Are there alternative tests to the TST?
There are two kinds of tests that are used to determine if
a person has been infected with TB bacteria: the TB blood
test and the TB skin test. TB blood tests (sometimes called
IGRAs) use a blood sample to find TB infection. The tests
measure the response of TB proteins when they are mixed
with a small amount of blood. Only one visit is required to
draw blood for this test. Health care providers are encouraged
to use newer TB blood tests to screen for TB infection. In
order to prevent false-positive reactions, TB blood tests are
also the preferred method of TB testing for people 5 years of
age and older who have received the BCG TB vaccine.

Who can administer and read TB skin tests?
The TB skin test should be placed (administered) and read by a designated, trained health care provider. Consult with your state and local public health authorities to determine who is authorized to place and read TB skin tests in your state.
TB skin test training materials
Training is essential for health care providers to gain proficiency in the administration and interpretation of the TB skin test.
CDC has free training materials on reading and administering the TB skin test, including a fact sheet, wall chart, and video. Materials are available for download or to order (within the United States).
Keep Reading:
Mantoux Tuberculin Skin Test Toolkit
Determining an approach
CDC has resources to help health care providers talk to patients about TB testing and treatment.
CDC guidelines recommend using TB blood tests to test for TB infection in most cases. However, TB skin tests are an acceptable alternative in situations where a TB blood test is not available, is too costly, or is too burdensome.

quotes.whole:
After 48–72 hours, the skin test reaction must be examined by a trained health care worker. The health care worker measures the induration (firm swelling) where the tuberculin was injected to determine if the reaction to the test is positive or negative.
Keep Reading:
Clinical Testing Guidance for Tuberculosis: Tuberculin Skin Test
Selecting a test to detect TB infection
Using either a TB blood test or a TB skin test is acceptable medical and public health practice.
Health care providers are encouraged to use newer TB blood tests to detect latent TB infection.  TB skin tests are an acceptable alternative in situations where a TB blood test is not available, is too costly, or is too burdensome.
The bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) TB vaccine can cause a false positive TB skin test result. Unlike the TB skin test, TB blood tests are not affected by BCG vaccination.
Routine testing with both TB blood and skin tests is not recommended.
Consider these factors when determining which test to use.
TB blood test is the preferred method of testing for:
People who have received the BCG vaccine
People who might be less likely to return for TB skin test reading and interpretation

verdict.summary:
DRAFT FOR QUALIFIED CLINICIAN REVIEW ONLY — NOT MEDICAL ADVICE AND NOT FOR PATIENT CARE.

1. Summary Answers
- When the tuberculin skin test (TST) reaction must be examined: 48–72 hours after administration (placement) [CDC, Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Tuberculosis, Apr. 17, 2025; CDC, Clinical Testing Guidance for Tuberculosis: Tuberculin Skin Test, Jan. 31, 2025]. If a patient does not return within 72 hours, they must be rescheduled for another skin test [CDC, Tuberculin Skin Testing Information for Health Care Providers].
- Who must examine it: A trained health care worker (also referred to in the interpretation section as a trained health care professional or designated, trained health care provider) [CDC, Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Tuberculosis, Apr. 17, 2025; CDC, Clinical Testing Guidance for Tuberculosis: Tuberculin Skin Test, Jan. 31, 2025]. Because authorization varies by jurisdiction, providers should consult state and local public health authorities to determine who is authorized to place and read TB skin tests in their state [CDC, Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Tuberculosis, Apr. 17, 2025; CDC, Clinical Testing Guidance for Tuberculosis: Tuberculin Skin Test, Jan. 31, 2025].

2. Clinical Context, Population, and Exposure
- Population: CDC recommends testing people who are at increased risk for tuberculosis (TB) infection [CDC, Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Tuberculosis, Apr. 17, 2025]. CDC guidelines recommend TB blood tests (interferon-gamma release assays) in most cases, but the TST is an acceptable alternative when a TB blood test is unavailable, too costly, or too burdensome, and is the current CDC-recommended method for children younger than 5 years of age (noting some experts use TB blood tests in younger children per American Academy of Pediatrics guidance) [CDC, Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Tuberculosis, Apr. 17, 2025; CDC, Clinical Testing Guidance for Tuberculosis: Tuberculin Skin Test, Jan. 31, 2025].
- Dose and Exposure: The Mantoux TST is administered by intradermal injection of 0.1 mL of tuberculin purified protein derivative (PPD) into the inner surface of the forearm using a tuberculin syringe with the needle bevel facing upward, which should produce a pale skin elevation (wheal) measuring 6 to 10 millimeters (mm) in diameter when placed correctly [CDC, Tuberculin Skin Testing Information for Health Care Providers].

3. Examination and Measurement Procedure
- At 48–72 hours after injection, the trained health care worker examines the injection site and measures induration (firm swelling) across the forearm (perpendicular to the long axis) in millimeters (mm), without measuring erythema (redness) [CDC, Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Tuberculosis, Apr. 17, 2025; CDC, Tuberculin Skin Testing Information for Health Care Providers].
- Interpretation of the reaction as positive or negative depends on the induration measurement in mm, the person's risk of acquiring TB infection, and the risk of progression to TB disease if infected (for example, an induration of 10 mm or more is positive in people born in countries where TB disease is common, and 15 mm or more is positive in people with no known TB risk factors) [CDC, Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Tuberculosis, Apr. 17, 2025; CDC, Clinical Testing Guidance for Tuberculosis: Tuberculin Skin Test, Jan. 31, 2025].

4. Evidence Limitations and Source Note
- Source Currency Note: The request specifies the CDC page available on 2026-11-21; the retrieved CDC webpage is dated April 17, 2025, and was fetched on 2026-11-22T23:33:46Z (confirming its active content immediately following 2026-11-21).
- Terminological and Jurisdictional Variation: The primary CDC page uses both "trained health care worker" (in the 48–72 hour examination statement) and "trained health care professional" (in the interpretation section), while the linked TST guidance page refers to a "designated, trained health care provider" and "health care worker trained to read TB skin results." The CDC guidance does not define a uniform national credential; legal authorization is explicitly deferred to state and local public health authorities.

5. Full Citations
1. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Tuberculosis. Updated April 17, 2025. https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/index.html (fetched 2026-11-22T23:33:46Z, sha256 9095c1db7f3e).
2. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Clinical Testing Guidance for Tuberculosis: Tuberculin Skin Test. Updated January 31, 2025. https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/tuberculin-skin-test.html (fetched 2026-11-22T23:33:46Z, sha256 4aa43e3065d3).
3. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Tuberculin Skin Testing Information for Health Care Providers. https://www.cdc.gov/tb/publications/factsheets/testing/Tuberculin_Skin_Testing_Information_for_Health_Care_Providers.pdf (fetched 2026-11-22T23:33:47Z, sha256 8e42decc7a4c).
4. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Latent Tuberculosis Infection: A Guide for Primary Health Care Providers. https://www.cdc.gov/tb/media/pdfs/latent-tb-infection-a-guide-for-primary-health-care-providers.pdf (fetched 2026-11-22T23:33:49Z, sha256 8810c24b1e6a).

Tuberculin Skin Testing
What is it?
The Mantoux tuberculin skin test (TST) is one method
of determining whether a person is infected with
Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Reliable administration
and reading of the TST requires standardization of
procedures, training, supervision, and practice.
How is the TST Administered?
The TST is performed by injecting 0.1 ml of tuberculin
purified protein derivative (PPD) into the inner surface
of the forearm. The injection should be made with a
tuberculin syringe, with the needle bevel facing upward.
The TST is an intradermal injection. When placed
correctly,

• Either on the same day as vaccination with live-virus
vaccine or
• At least 1 month after the administration of the live-virus
vaccine
Are there alternative tests to the TST?
There are two kinds of tests that are used to determine if
a person has been infected with TB bacteria: the TB blood
test and the TB skin test. TB blood tests (sometimes called
IGRAs) use a blood sample to find TB infection. The tests

A patient who does not return within 72 hours will need to be rescheduled for another skin test.

Health care providers are encouraged to use newer TB blood tests to screen for TB infection. In order to prevent false-positive reactions, TB blood tests are also the preferred method of TB testing for people 5 years of age and older who have received the BCG TB vaccine.

quotes.whole:
§ 814.42 Filing a PMA.




(a) The filing of an application means that FDA has made a threshold determination that the application is sufficiently complete to permit a substantive review. Within 45 days after a PMA is received by FDA, the agency will notify the applicant whether the application has been filed.






(b) If FDA does not find that any of the reasons in paragraph (e) of this section for refusing to file the PMA applies, the agency will file the PMA and will notify the applicant in writing of the filing. The notice will include the PMA reference number and the date FDA filed the PMA. The date of filing is the date that a PMA accepted for filing was received by the agency. The 180-day period for review of a PMA starts on the date of filing.






(c) If FDA refuses to file a PMA, the agency will notify the applicant of the reasons for the refusal. This notice will identify the deficiencies in the application that prevent filing and will include the PMA reference number.






(d) If FDA refuses to file the PMA, the applicant may:




(1) Resubmit the PMA with additional information necessary to comply with the requirements of section 515(c)(1) (A)-(G) of the act and § 814.20. A resubmitted PMA shall include the PMA reference number of the original submission. If the resubmitted PMA is accepted for filing, the date of filing is the date FDA receives the resubmission;






(2) Request in writing within 10 working days of the date of receipt of the notice refusing to file the PMA, an informal conference with the Director of the associated Office of Health Technology to review FDA's decision not to file the PMA. FDA will hold the informal conference within 10 working days of its receipt of the request and will render its decision on filing within 5 working days after the informal conference. If, after the informal conference, FDA accepts the PMA for filing, the date of filing will be the date of the decision to accept the PMA for filing. If FDA does not reverse its decision not to file the PMA, the applicant may request reconsideration of the decision from the Director of the Office of Product Evaluation and Quality, the Director of the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research, or the Director of the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, as applicable. The Director's decision will constitute final administrative action for the purpose of judicial review.








(e) FDA may refuse to file a PMA if any of the following applies:




(1) The application is incomplete because it does not on its face contain all the information required under section 515(c)(1) (A)-(G) of the act;






(2) The PMA does not contain each of the items required under § 814.20 and justification for omission of any item is inadequate;






(3) The applicant has a pending premarket notification under section 510(k) of the act with respect to the same device, and FDA has not determined whether the device falls within the scope of § 814.1(c).






(4) The PMA contains a false statement of material fact.





(5) The PMA is not accompanied by a statement of either certification or disclosure as required by part 54 of this chapter.





[51 FR 26364, July 22, 1986, as amended at 63 FR 5254, Feb. 2, 1998; 73 FR 49942, Aug. 25, 2008; 85 FR 18442, Apr. 2, 2020]

quotes.whole:
§ 814.42 Filing a PMA.




(a) The filing of an application means that FDA has made a threshold determination that the application is sufficiently complete to permit a substantive review. Within 45 days after a PMA is received by FDA, the agency will notify the applicant whether the application has been filed.






(b) If FDA does not find that any of the reasons in paragraph (e) of this section for refusing to file the PMA applies, the agency will file the PMA and will notify the applicant in writing of the filing. The notice will include the PMA reference number and the date FDA filed the PMA. The date of filing is the date that a PMA accepted for filing was received by the agency. The 180-day period for review of a PMA starts on the date of filing.






(c) If FDA refuses to file a PMA, the agency will notify the applicant of the reasons for the refusal. This notice will identify the deficiencies in the application that prevent filing and will include the PMA reference number.






(d) If FDA refuses to file the PMA, the applicant may:




(1) Resubmit the PMA with additional information necessary to comply with the requirements of section 515(c)(1) (A)-(G) of the act and § 814.20. A resubmitted PMA shall include the PMA reference number of the original submission. If the resubmitted PMA is accepted for filing, the date of filing is the date FDA receives the resubmission;






(2) Request in writing within 10 working days of the date of receipt of the notice refusing to file the PMA, an informal conference with the Director of the associated Office of Health Technology to review FDA's decision not to file the PMA. FDA will hold the informal conference within 10 working days of its receipt of the request and will render its decision on filing within 5 working days after the informal conference. If, after the informal conference, FDA accepts the PMA for filing, the date of filing will be the date of the decision to accept the PMA for filing. If FDA does not reverse its decision not to file the PMA, the applicant may request reconsideration of the decision from the Director of the Office of Product Evaluation and Quality, the Director of the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research, or the Director of the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, as applicable. The Director's decision will constitute final administrative action for the purpose of judicial review.








(e) FDA may refuse to file a PMA if any of the following applies:




(1) The application is incomplete because it does not on its face contain all the information required under section 515(c)(1) (A)-(G) of the act;






(2) The PMA does not contain each of the items required under § 814.20 and justification for omission of any item is inadequate;






(3) The applicant has a pending premarket notification under section 510(k) of the act with respect to the same device, and FDA has not determined whether the device falls within the scope of § 814.1(c).






(4) The PMA contains a false statement of material fact.





(5) The PMA is not accompanied by a statement of either certification or disclosure as required by part 54 of this chapter.

1. Direct Answer
Under 21 CFR § 814.42(a) (Title 21, Chapter I, Subchapter H, Part 814, Subpart C — FDA Actions on Applications, as in force on 2026-11-21), FDA must notify the applicant whether a Premarket Approval (PMA) application has been filed within 45 days after the PMA is received by FDA.

2. Applicability (Population and Exposure)
- Applicable Population / Scope: Original Premarket Approval (PMA) applications for medical devices subject to PMA requirements (and their applicants) submitted to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) under 21 CFR Part 814. Note: Humanitarian Device Exemption (HDE) applications follow a separate 30-day filing-notification timeframe under 21 CFR Part 814 (Subpart H).
- Clinical Dose / Exposure: Not applicable (this regulatory determination addresses administrative filing timelines rather than a therapeutic intervention or clinical exposure).

3. Authoritative Regulatory Text and Citation
- Primary Source Cited in Full: 21 CFR Part 814, Subpart C, § 814.42 ("Filing a PMA"), Electronic Code of Federal Regulations (eCFR), Title 21, Chapter I, Subchapter H (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-H/part-814/subpart-C/section-814.42; fetched 2026-11-22T23:38:14Z, reflecting text in force on 2026-11-21). History: 51 FR 26364, July 22, 1986, as amended at 63 FR 5254, Feb. 2, 1998; 73 FR 49942, Aug. 25, 2008; 85 FR 18442, Apr. 2, 2020. Corroborated by 21 CFR § 814.42, 2025 CFR Title 21, Volume 8 (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title21-vol8/pdf/CFR-2025-title21-vol8-sec814-42.pdf; fetched 2026-11-22T23:38:15Z).
- Verbatim Regulatory Language (21 CFR § 814.42(a)):
  "The filing of an application means that FDA has made a threshold determination that the application is sufficiently complete to permit a substantive review. Within 45 days after a PMA is received by FDA, the agency will notify the applicant whether the application has been filed."

4. Procedural Distinctions and Related Timelines (21 CFR § 814.42)
- Filing Determination vs. Approval Review: The 45-day threshold filing notification is distinct from substantive approval review. Under 21 CFR § 814.42(b), if no grounds for refusal under § 814.42(e) apply, FDA will notify the applicant in writing of the filing (including the PMA reference number and filing date). The date of filing is the date that an accepted PMA was received by FDA, and the 180-day period for substantive review of the PMA starts on that date of filing (21 CFR § 814.42(b)).
- Note on Day Counting: 21 CFR § 814.42(a) specifies "45 days" without the "working days" qualifier used in § 814.42(d)(2); where working days are intended, § 814.42 explicitly specifies "working days."
- Refusal to File (21 CFR § 814.42(c)–(e)): FDA may refuse to file a PMA if any criterion in § 814.42(e)(1)–(5) applies (e.g., facial incompleteness under section 515(c)(1)(A)–(G) of the Act, missing § 814.20 items without adequate justification, pending 510(k) without a § 814.1(c) determination, false statement of material fact, or missing 21 CFR Part 54 financial certification/disclosure). If FDA refuses to file, it notifies the applicant of the reasons and identifying deficiencies (§ 814.42(c)).
- Applicant Options Following Refusal to File (21 CFR § 814.42(d)):
  1. Resubmit the PMA with additional required information under section 515(c)(1)(A)–(G) of the Act and § 814.20, referencing the original PMA number; if accepted, the filing date is the date FDA receives the resubmission (§ 814.42(d)(1)).
  2. Request in writing, within 10 working days of receipt of the refusal-to-file notice, an informal conference with the Director of the associated Office of Health Technology. FDA will hold the conference within 10 working days of receipt of the request and render a filing decision within 5 working days after the conference (§ 814.42(d)(2)). If accepted after the conference, the filing date is the date of the decision to accept; if not reversed, the applicant may request reconsideration from the applicable Center/Office Director, whose decision constitutes final administrative action for judicial review (§ 814.42(d)(2)).

"AAMI/ISO 13485:2016, A Practical Guide" (PDF)
"AAMI TIR102:2019, U.S. FDA 21 CFR mapping to the applicable regulatory requirement references in ISO 13485:2016 Quality Management Systems"
On January 31, 2024, the FDA issued a final rule amending the device current good manufacturing practice (CGMP) requirements of the Quality System (QS) Regulation under 21 CFR 820 to align more closely with the international consensus standard for Quality Management Systems for medical devices used by many other regulatory authorities around the world.
This rule amends 21 CFR 820 by incorporating by reference the quality management system requirements of the international standard specific for medical device quality management systems set by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO), ISO 13485:2016. The FDA has determined that the requirements in ISO 13485 are, when taken in totality, substantially similar to the requirements of the QS regulation, providing a similar level of assurance in a firm’s quality management system and ability to consistently manufacture devices that are safe and effective and otherwise in compliance with the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act).

verdict.summary:
DRAFT FOR QUALIFIED REGULATORY AND CLINICAL QUALITY REVIEW — NOT MEDICAL OR LEGAL ADVICE AND NOT FOR PATIENT CARE.

1. Exact ISO 13485 Edition and Edition Date Incorporated by Reference (as in force on 2026-11-21)
- Standard Designation and Edition: ISO 13485:2016(E) (“ISO 13485”), Medical devices—Quality management systems—Requirements for regulatory purposes, Third edition, March 1, 2016 (also cited as 2016-03-01 in the rulemaking preamble).
- Codified Location: 21 CFR § 820.7(b) (Incorporation by reference), approved by the Director of the Federal Register under 5 U.S.C. 552(a) and 1 CFR part 51, for §§ 820.1, 820.3, 820.10, 820.35, and 820.45.
- Legacy Manual Status: The legacy quality manual's citation to ISO 13485:2003 is obsolete and non-compliant with 21 CFR Part 820 as in force on 2026-11-21.

2. Regulatory Scope, Population, and Effective Date Verification
- Regulated Population / Scope: Manufacturers of medical devices subject to 21 CFR Part 820 (Quality Management System Regulation [QMSR]) as described in 21 CFR § 820.1(a). No patient clinical dosing or therapeutic exposure applies to this regulatory standards determination.
- Rulemaking & Effective Date Basis: On January 31, 2024, FDA issued the final rule "Medical Devices; Quality System Regulation Amendments" (89 FR 7496; FR Doc. 2024-01709, published February 2, 2024). Per FDA's Quality Management System Regulation (QMSR) Frequently Asked Questions (Question 6), the rule became effective February 2, 2026 (two years after Federal Register publication), at which time FDA began enforcing QMSR requirements and withdrew the Quality System Inspection Technique (QSIT) in favor of Inspection of Medical Device Manufacturers Compliance Program 7382.850. Because February 2, 2026 precedes November 21, 2026, and the live eCFR text of 21 CFR Part 820 (retrieved 2026-11-22T23:41:32Z) retains § 820.7(b) unchanged, ISO 13485:2016(E), Third edition, March 1, 2016 is the exact edition in force on 2026-11-21.

3. Exact Codified Language and Companion Incorporations for Quality Manual Revision
- Primary IBR Text (21 CFR § 820.7(b)): "ISO 13485:2016(E) (“ISO 13485”), Medical devices—Quality management systems—Requirements for regulatory purposes, Third edition, March 1, 2016; IBR approved for §§ 820.1, 820.3, 820.10, 820.35, and 820.45."
- Companion Terms and Definitions IBR (21 CFR § 820.7(a)): "ISO 9000:2015(E) (“ISO 9000”), Quality Management systems—Fundamentals and vocabulary, Clause 3—Terms and definitions, Fourth edition, September 15, 2015. IBR approved for § 820.3."
- Required Quality Manual Updates Beyond Edition Number:
  1) Replace all references to ISO 13485:2003 (and pre-2026 QS Regulation section numbers) with ISO 13485:2016(E), Third edition, March 1, 2016, and reference Clause 3 of ISO 9000:2015(E), Fourth edition, September 15, 2015 for baseline definitions, noting FDA superseding definitions in 21 CFR § 820.3(b) (e.g., "implantable medical device" takes the meaning of "implant" under 21 CFR § 860.3).
  2) Document compliance with QMSR supplemental provisions in 21 CFR Part 820 that apply in addition to ISO 13485:2016: § 820.1(d) (devices supporting or sustaining life must comply with ISO 13485 Clause 7.5.9.2, Traceability for Implantable Devices), § 820.10(b)(1) (ISO 13485 Clause 7.5.8 requires Unique Device Identification [UDI] under 21 CFR Part 830), § 820.35 (supplemental record requirements for complaints, servicing under Clause 7.5.4, and UDI recording under Clauses 7.5.1, 7.5.8, and 7.5.9), and § 820.45 (supplemental labeling and packaging controls beyond Clause 7.5.1).
  3) Note that failure to comply with applicable Part 820 requirements renders a device adulterated under section 501(h) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 CFR § 820.1(e)). If the device is also marketed outside the United States (e.g., under EU MDR), applicable regional standards (such as EN ISO 13485) should be verified separately.

4. Full Source Citations

- U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Final Rule: Medical Devices; Quality System Regulation Amendments, 89 FR 7496 (FR Doc. 2024-01709, published February 2, 2024; effective February 2, 2026), https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2024/02/02/2024-01709/medical-devices-quality-system-regulation-amendments.
- U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Quality Management System Regulation: Frequently Asked Questions (QMSR FAQ), Questions 4–7, 11–12, https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/quality-management-system-regulation-qmsr/quality-management-system-regulation-frequently-asked-questions (retrieved 2026-11-22T23:41:32Z).

quotes.whole:
Editorial Note on Part 860




Editorial Note:


Nomenclature changes to part 860 appear at 73 FR 35341, June 23, 2008, and at 86 FR 54846, Oct. 5, 2021.






§ 860.230 Accepting a De Novo request.




(a) The acceptance of a De Novo request means that FDA has made a threshold determination that the De Novo request contains the information necessary to permit a substantive review. Within 15 days after a De Novo request is received by FDA, FDA will notify the requester whether the De Novo request has been accepted.






(b) If FDA does not find that any of the reasons in paragraph (c)(1) of this section for refusing to accept the De Novo request apply or FDA fails to complete the acceptance review within 15 days, FDA will accept the De Novo request for review and will notify the requester. The notice will include the De Novo request reference number and the date FDA accepted the De Novo request. The date of acceptance is the date that an accepted De Novo request was received by FDA.






(c) 




(1) FDA may refuse to accept a De Novo request if any of the following applies:




(i) The requester has an open or pending premarket submission or reclassification petition for the device;






(ii) The De Novo request is incomplete because it does not on its face contain all the information required under section 513(f)(2) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act or does not contain each of the items required under this part, or a justification for omission of any item;






(iii) The De Novo request is not formatted as required under § 860.210;






(iv) The De Novo request is for multiple devices and those devices are of more than one type; or






(v) The requester has not responded to, or has failed to provide a rationale for not responding to, deficiencies identified by FDA in previous submissions for the same device, including those submissions described in § 860.220(a)(3).








(2) If FDA refuses to accept a De Novo request, FDA will notify the requester of the reasons for the refusal. The notice will identify the deficiencies in the De Novo request that prevent accepting and will include the De Novo request reference number.





(3) If FDA refuses to accept a De Novo request, the requester may submit the additional information necessary to comply with the requirements of section 513(f)(2) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and this part. The additional information must include the De Novo request reference number of the original submission. If the De Novo request is subsequently accepted, the date of acceptance is the date FDA receives the additional information.
