quotes.whole:
Editorial Note on Part 860




Editorial Note:


Nomenclature changes to part 860 appear at 73 FR 35341, June 23, 2008, and at 86 FR 54846, Oct. 5, 2021.






§ 860.240 Procedures for review of a De Novo request.




(a) FDA will begin substantive review of a De Novo request after the De Novo request is accepted under § 860.230. Within 120 days after receipt of a De Novo request or receipt of additional information that results in the De Novo request being accepted under § 860.230, FDA will review the De Novo request and send the requester an order granting the De Novo request under § 860.260(a) or an order declining the De Novo request under 860.260(b).






(b) A requester may supplement or amend a pending De Novo request to revise existing information or provide additional information.




(1) FDA may require additional information regarding the device that is necessary for FDA to complete the review of the De Novo request.






(2) Additional information submitted to FDA must include the reference number assigned to the original De Novo request and, if submitted on the requester's own initiative, the reason for submitting the additional information.








(c) Prior to granting or declining a De Novo request, FDA may inspect relevant facilities to help determine:




(1) That clinical or nonclinical data were collected in a manner that ensures that the data accurately represents the benefits and risks of the device; or





(2) That implementation of Quality Management System Regulation (part 820 of this chapter) requirements, in addition to other general controls and any specified special controls, provide adequate assurance that critical and/or novel manufacturing processes produce devices that meet specifications necessary to ensure reasonable assurance of safety and effectiveness.





[86 FR 54847, Oct. 5, 2021, as amended at 90 FR 55980, Dec. 4, 2025]

Editorial Note on Part 860




Editorial Note:


Nomenclature changes to part 860 appear at 73 FR 35341, June 23, 2008, and at 86 FR 54846, Oct. 5, 2021.






§ 860.250 Withdrawal of a De Novo request.




(a) FDA considers a De Novo request to have been withdrawn if:




(1) The requester fails to provide a complete response to a request for additional information pursuant to § 860.240(b)(1) within 180 days after the date FDA issues such request;






(2) The requester fails to provide a complete response to the deficiencies identified by FDA pursuant to § 860.230(c)(2) within 180 days of the date notification was issued by FDA;






(3) The requester does not permit an authorized FDA employee an opportunity to inspect the facilities, pursuant to § 860.240(c), at a reasonable time and in a reasonable manner, and to have access to copy and verify all records pertinent to the De Novo request; or






(4) The requester submits a written notice to FDA that the De Novo request has been withdrawn.







(b) If a De Novo request is withdrawn, the Agency will notify the requester. The notice will include the De Novo request reference number and the date FDA considered the De Novo request withdrawn.

The Commissioner, in the Commissioner's discretion, may allow withdrawal of a deficient petition during the 30-day period provided for correcting deficiencies. (1) FDA may refuse to accept a De Novo request if any of the following applies:




(i) The requester has an open or pending premarket submission or reclassification petition for the device;






(ii) The De Novo request is incomplete because it does not on its face contain all the information required under section 513(f)(2) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act or does not contain each of the items required under this part, or a justification for omission of any item;






(iii) The De Novo request is not formatted as required under § 860.210;






(iv) The De Novo request is for multiple devices and those devices are of more than one type; or






(v) The requester has not responded to, or has failed to provide a rationale for not responding to, deficiencies identified by FDA in previous submissions for the same device, including those submissions described in § 860.220(a)(3).








(2) If FDA refuses to accept a De Novo request, FDA will notify the requester of the reasons for the refusal. The notice will identify the deficiencies in the De Novo request that prevent accepting and will include the De Novo request reference number.





(3) If FDA refuses to accept a De Novo request, the requester may submit the additional information necessary to comply with the requirements of section 513(f)(2) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and this part. The additional information must include the De Novo request reference number of the original submission. If the De Novo request is subsequently accepted, the date of acceptance is the date FDA receives the additional information.

§ 860.240 Procedures for review of a De Novo request.




(a) FDA will begin substantive review of a De Novo request after the De Novo request is accepted under § 860.230. (b) A requester may supplement or amend a pending De Novo request to revise existing information or provide additional information.




(1) FDA may require additional information regarding the device that is necessary for FDA to complete the review of the De Novo request.






(2) Additional information submitted to FDA must include the reference number assigned to the original De Novo request and, if submitted on the requester's own initiative, the reason for submitting the additional information.








(c) Prior to granting or declining a De Novo request, FDA may inspect relevant facilities to help determine:




(1) That clinical or nonclinical data were collected in a manner that ensures that the data accurately represents the benefits and risks of the device; or





(2) That implementation of Quality Management System Regulation (part 820 of this chapter) requirements, in addition to other general controls and any specified special controls, provide adequate assurance that critical and/or novel manufacturing processes produce devices that meet specifications necessary to ensure reasonable assurance of safety and effectiveness.

verdict.summary:
DRAFT FOR QUALIFIED CLINICIAN REVIEW ONLY. This regulatory summary is not medical advice, is not legal advice, and is not for patient care.

### Regulatory Time Limits for a De Novo Request Accepted Without Additional-Information Submission
Under **21 CFR Part 860, Subpart D (De Novo Classification)**, as in force on **2026-11-21** (verified against the eCFR current as fetched 2026-11-22T23:45:13Z; 86 FR 54846–54847, Oct. 5, 2021, with 21 CFR § 860.240 amended at 90 FR 55980, Dec. 4, 2025):

1. **Outside Time Limit for Acceptance Notification: 15 days**
   - **Figure and Unit:** `15 days` (the regulation uses "days" without specifying business or working days, corresponding to calendar days).
   - **Trigger / Clock Start:** Date the De Novo request is received by FDA.
   - **Governing Provision:** **21 CFR § 860.230(a)–(b)** (*Accepting a De Novo request*, eCFR current as of 2026-11-22; editorial note citing 73 FR 35341, June 23, 2008, and 86 FR 54846, Oct. 5, 2021).
   - **Regulatory Requirement:** Under § 860.230(a), within **15 days** after a De Novo request is received by FDA, FDA must notify the requester whether the De Novo request has been accepted (i.e., that FDA has made a threshold determination that the submission contains the information necessary to permit substantive review). Under § 860.230(b), if FDA does not find that any refusal-to-accept grounds in § 860.230(c)(1) apply—or if FDA fails to complete the acceptance review within **15 days**—FDA will accept the De Novo request for review and notify the requester. The notice includes the De Novo request reference number and the date of acceptance, which is the date the accepted De Novo request was received by FDA.

2. **Outside Time Limit for FDA's Substantive Review and Granting or Declining Order: 120 days**
   - **Figure and Unit:** `120 days` (stated as "days" in the regulation).
   - **Trigger / Clock Start:** Date of FDA's receipt of the De Novo request (because the request is accepted without any additional-information submission under § 860.230(c)(3)).
   - **Governing Provision:** **21 CFR § 860.240(a)** (*Procedures for review of a De Novo request*, 86 FR 54847, Oct. 5, 2021, as amended at 90 FR 55980, Dec. 4, 2025), cross-referencing **21 CFR § 860.260(a)** (order granting) and **21 CFR § 860.260(b)** (order declining).
   - **Regulatory Requirement:** Under § 860.240(a), FDA begins substantive review after the De Novo request is accepted under § 860.230. Within **120 days** after receipt of the De Novo request (or receipt of additional information resulting in acceptance under § 860.230, which does not apply here), FDA will review the De Novo request and send the requester an order granting the De Novo request under § 860.260(a) or an order declining the De Novo request under § 860.260(b).
   - **Important Clock Relationship:** The **120-day** limit is measured from FDA's receipt of the original De Novo request—not 120 days added on top of the 15-day acceptance period—consistent with § 860.230(b), which sets the acceptance date as the receipt date.

### Scope and Contextual Notes from 21 CFR Part 860, Subpart D
- **Acceptance Without Additional-Information Submission:** Because the request is accepted on the initial filing without a refusal-to-accept under § 860.230(c)(1)–(2) and without an additional-information submission under § 860.230(c)(3), the alternative acceptance-date and review-clock-start rules triggered by receipt of acceptance-stage additional information do not apply.
- **Substantive-Review Interactions:** During substantive review, 21 CFR § 860.240(b) permits the requester to supplement or amend a pending De Novo request and authorizes FDA to require additional information necessary to complete review (§ 860.240(b)(1)); failure to provide a complete response to a § 860.240(b)(1) request within **180 days** after issuance results in deemed withdrawal under **21 CFR § 860.250(a)(1)**. Additionally, under § 860.240(c) (as amended at 90 FR 55980, Dec. 4, 2025), FDA may inspect relevant facilities prior to granting or declining the request to verify clinical/nonclinical data collection integrity or Quality Management System Regulation (21 CFR Part 820) compliance. The scenario analyzed here assumes no post-acceptance additional-information submission or withdrawal occurs, leaving the statutory/regulatory outside limits in § 860.230(a)–(b) and § 860.240(a) at **15 days** and **120 days**, respectively.
- **Source Identification:**
  - 21 CFR § 860.230 (*Accepting a De Novo request*), eCFR current as of 2026-11-22 (reflecting 86 FR 54846, Oct. 5, 2021).
  - 21 CFR § 860.240 (*Procedures for review of a De Novo request*), eCFR current as of 2026-11-22 (86 FR 54847, Oct. 5, 2021, as amended at 90 FR 55980, Dec. 4, 2025).
  - 21 CFR § 860.250 (*Withdrawal of a De Novo request*) and § 860.260 (*Granting or declining a De Novo request*), eCFR current as of 2026-11-22.

The Note for Guidance on Clinical Safety Data Management: Definitions and Standards for Expedited Reporting (CPMP/ICH/377/95) is an internationally accepted standard for the reporting of important clinical safety information principally arising during clinical development of medicines.
The TGA has adopted the Note for Guidance on Clinical Safety Data Management: Definitions and Standards for Expedited Reporting in principle, particularly its definitions and reporting time frames. However, there are some elements of CPMP/ICH/377/95 which have not been adopted by the TGA and other elements which require explanation in terms of 'local regulatory requirements'.

verdict.summary:
DRAFT FOR QUALIFIED CLINICIAN REVIEW — NOT MEDICAL ADVICE AND NOT FOR PATIENT CARE.

1. Regulatory Determination and Timeline Calculation
Under the International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) Harmonised Tripartite Guideline E2A, "Clinical Safety Data Management: Definitions and Standards for Expedited Reporting" (Current Step 4 version dated 27 October 1994; new codification November 2005), Section III.B.1 ("Fatal or Life-Threatening Unexpected ADRs"):
- Outer limit for initial regulatory notification (Ask 1): 7 calendar days after Day 0 (i.e., no later than Day 7, where Day 0 is the date of first knowledge by the sponsor that the case qualifies for the 7-day expedited reporting rule).
- Follow-up report deadline when the full initial period is used (Ask 2 constraint & Ask 3): Day 15 measured from Day 0 (15 calendar days from Day 0), calculated as 7 calendar days for initial notification plus 8 additional calendar days for the complete follow-up report (7 calendar days + 8 calendar days = 15 calendar days).

2. Governing Source Text and Scope (Population and Exposure)
- Applicable Population and Exposure: Clinical investigation subjects exposed to an investigational medicinal product (no specific medicinal product, dose, formulation, or patient cohort was provided in the request). Per ICH E2A (Step 4, 27 October 1994), this 7-calendar-day expedited reporting rule applies specifically to fatal or life-threatening, unexpected adverse drug reactions (ADRs) occurring in clinical investigations. (By contrast, under ICH E2A Section III.B.2, all other serious, unexpected ADRs that are not fatal or life-threatening must be filed as soon as possible, no later than 15 calendar days after first knowledge that minimum reporting criteria are met; post-approval single-case 15-calendar-day expedited reporting is addressed in ICH E2D, "Post-Approval Safety Data Management: Definitions and Standards for Expedited Reporting," version 3.8 dated 18 July 2003, Section 3.2.)
- Verbatim Governing Standard (ICH E2A, Step 4, 27 October 1994; also published in Health Canada Guidance for Industry, ICH Topic E2A, 1995, p. 7): "Fatal or life-threatening, unexpected ADRs occurring in clinical investigations qualify for very rapid reporting. Regulatory agencies should be notified (e.g., by telephone, facsimile transmission, or in writing) as soon as possible but no later than 7 calendar days after first knowledge by the sponsor that a case qualifies, followed by as complete a report as possible within 8 additional calendar days. This report must include an assessment of the importance and implication of the findings, including relevant previous experience with the same or similar medicinal products."

3. Operational Clock-Start, Counting Rules, and Deliverable Content
- Day 0 Definition: Day 0 is the calendar date on which the sponsor first has knowledge that the case meets the qualifying criteria for the 7-day expedited rule (minimum reporting criteria plus fatal or life-threatening seriousness, unexpectedness, and suspected causal relationship to the investigational product).
- Counting Convention: All time limits in ICH E2A are measured in calendar days (not business days). Using exclusive day-counting from Day 0 (Day 0 + 7 calendar days = Day 7), if the sponsor notifies regulatory agencies on Day 7, the follow-up report is due within 8 additional calendar days, which is Day 15 measured from Day 0 (Day 7 + 8 calendar days = Day 15).
- Required Initial Notification Modes: Telephone, facsimile transmission, or in writing (or electronic submission per local agency requirements), submitted as soon as possible and no later than Day 7.
- Required Follow-Up Report Content (Due by Day 15 if notified on Day 7): As complete a case report as possible, explicitly including an assessment of the clinical importance and implication of the findings and relevant previous experience with the same or similar medicinal products.
- Regional Transposition Note: While ICH E2A (Step 4, 27 October 1994) establishes the 7-calendar-day and 8-additional-calendar-day (Day 15 total) framework—adopted, for example, by Health Canada (Guidance for Industry ICH Topic E2A, 1995) and Australia TGA (CPMP/ICH/377/95, overseas effective date June 1995)—sponsors must confirm jurisdiction-specific statutory rules (e.g., US FDA IND safety reporting or EU clinical trial reporting regulations) for any local variations in clock-start mechanics or electronic transmission format.

All adverse drug reactions (ADRs) that are both serious and unexpected are subject to expedited reporting. The following definitions, with input from the WHO Collaborative Centre, have been agreed:

1. Adverse Event (or Adverse Experience) Any untoward medical occurrence in a patient or clinical investigation subject administered a pharmaceutical product and which does not necessarily have to have a causal relationship with this treatment. An adverse event (AE) can therefore be any unfavourable and unintended sign (including an abnormal laboratory finding, for example), symptom, or disease temporally associated with the use of a medicinal product, whether or not considered related to the medicinal product.

Expedited reporting of reactions which are serious but expected will ordinarily be inappropriate. Expedited reporting is also inappropriate for serious events from clinical investigations that are considered not related to study product, whether the event is expected or not. Similarly, non-serious adverse reactions, whether expected or not, will ordinarily not be subject to expedited reporting.

verdict.summary:
DRAFT FOR QUALIFIED CLINICIAN AND REGULATORY REVIEW ONLY. This document is not medical advice and is not for patient care.

1. Regulatory Determination
The sponsor's next Investigational New Drug (IND) submission must carry the three-digit serial number 018.

2. Governing Regulation and Source Citation
- Citation: Title 21, Code of Federal Regulations, Part 312, Subpart B, Section 312.23(e) (21 CFR 312.23(e)), "IND content and format — Numbering of IND submissions," U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), Electronic Code of Federal Regulations (eCFR). (Note: The referenced eCFR excerpt text was not attached to the request, so its specific eCFR publication/revision date could not be independently verified from the prompt alone; this determination applies the codified text of 21 CFR 312.23(e).)
- Regulatory Requirement: Under 21 CFR 312.23(e), each submission relating to an IND must be numbered serially using a single, three-digit serial number. The initial IND is required to be numbered 000, and each subsequent submission (including protocol amendments, information amendments, IND safety reports, annual reports, or other correspondence) must be numbered chronologically in a single continuous sequence.

3. Serial Number Calculation
- Scope Parameters: Population = not applicable (administrative regulatory submission numbering task; no clinical population or drug dose/exposure specified). Units = submissions (count) and three-digit serial number (identifier).
- Initial IND submission (1 submission): Serial number 000.
- Subsequent IND submissions (17 submissions, numbered chronologically in sequence): Serial numbers 001 through 017 (1st later submission = 001; 17th later submission = 017).
- Next IND submission (18th later submission; 19th total submission in the IND lifecycle): 017 + 1 = 018.

4. Application Note for Submission Preparation
- Enter "018" in the Serial Number field of Form FDA 1571 (21 CFR 312.23(a)(1)), provided all 17 prior subsequent submissions were correctly numbered 001 through 017 with no skipped, duplicated, or parallel sequences.
- For operational awareness, if the IND is filed electronically in Electronic Common Technical Document (eCTD) format under FDA eCTD guidance ("Providing Regulatory Submissions in Electronic Format — Certain Human Pharmaceutical Product Applications and Related Submissions Using the eCTD Specifications"), eCTD uses four-digit sequence numbers starting at 0000; however, under the three-digit rule codified in 21 CFR 312.23(e) specified in this request, the required three-digit serial number is 018.

§ 807.81 When a premarket notification submission is required.




(a) Except as provided in paragraph (b) of this section, each person who is required to register his establishment pursuant to § 807.20 must submit a premarket notification submission to the Food and Drug Administration at least 90 days before he proposes to begin the introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution of a device intended for human use which meets any of the following criteria:




(1) The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time; that is, the device is not of the same type as, or is not substantially equivalent to, 



(i) a device in commercial distribution before May 28, 1976, or 





(ii) a device introduced for commercial distribution after May 28, 1976, that has subsequently been reclassified into class I or II.








(2) The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time by a person required to register, whether or not the device meets the criteria in paragraph (a)(1) of this section.






(3) The device is one that the person currently has in commercial distribution or is reintroducing into commercial distribution, but that is about to be significantly changed or modified in design, components, method of manufacture, or intended use. The following constitute significant changes or modifications that require a premarket notification:




(i) A change or modification in the device that could significantly affect the safety or effectiveness of the device, e.g., a significant change or modification in design, material, chemical composition, energy source, or manufacturing process.






(ii) A major change or modification in the intended use of the device.










(b) 




(1) A premarket notification under this subpart is not required for a device for which:




(i) A premarket approval application under section 515 of the act, or for which a petition to reclassify under section 513(f)(2) of the act, is pending before the Food and Drug Administration, or






(ii) There is a predetermined change control plan (PCCP) cleared under section 515C of the act, provided that the change is consistent with the PCCP.








(2) The appropriate FDA Center Director may determine that the submission and grant of a written request for an exception or alternative under § 801.128 or § 809.11 of this chapter satisfies the requirement in paragraph (a)(3) of this section.







(c) In addition to complying with the requirements of this part, owners or operators of device establishments that manufacture radiation-emitting electronic products, as defined in § 1000.3 of this chapter, shall comply with the reporting requirements of part 1002 of this chapter.

verdict.summary:
REGULATORY DETERMINATION: PREMARKET NOTIFICATION (510(k)) EXEMPTION FOR CUSTOM DEVICES

Disclaimer: This output is a draft regulatory analysis for review by a qualified clinician and regulatory affairs professional. It is not medical advice and is not intended for direct patient care.

1. Verdict
No. Under 21 CFR Part 807 Subpart E as in force on 2026-11-21, a manufacturer of a device that meets the custom-device meaning in section 520(b) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) is NOT required to submit a premarket notification (510(k)) at least 90 days before introducing or delivering the device into interstate commerce for commercial distribution, provided the conditions of 21 CFR 807.85(a) are satisfied.

2. Applicability Scope (Population, Exposure, and Jurisdictional Parameters)
- Target Population: Individual U.S. human patients named in the order of a physician, dentist, or other specially qualified person, or individual physicians, dentists, or other specially qualified persons using the device in the course of conducting their practice for a special need (21 CFR 807.85(a)(1)–(2); FD&C Act section 520(b)).
- Exposure / Regulatory Event: Introduction or delivery for introduction into U.S. interstate commerce for commercial distribution of a medical device intended for human use (21 CFR 807.81(a)).
- Evaluation Date: Regulatory text in force on 2026-11-21 (verified against eCFR fetched 2026-11-22T23:52:49Z and 2025 CFR Title 21, Volume 8).

3. Governing Regulations and Detailed Regulatory Analysis
- General Premarket Notification Rule (21 CFR 807.81(a); 42 FR 42526, Aug. 23, 1977, as amended at 72 FR 73601, Dec. 28, 2007; 89 FR 18792, Mar. 15, 2024): Each person required to register an establishment under 21 CFR 807.20 must submit a premarket notification to the FDA at least 90 days (time unit: days) before proposing to begin the introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution of a device intended for human use that is being introduced for the first time (not of the same type as, or substantially equivalent to, a device in commercial distribution before May 28, 1976, or reclassified into Class I or II thereafter), being introduced for the first time by that registrant, or undergoing a significant change or modification in design, components, method of manufacture, or intended use (unless an exception in 21 CFR 807.81(b) applies, such as a pending premarket approval application, reclassification petition, or cleared predetermined change control plan).
- Custom Device Exemption (21 CFR 807.85(a); 42 FR 42526, Aug. 23, 1977, as amended at 81 FR 70340, Oct. 12, 2016): Notwithstanding the 90-day requirement in 21 CFR 807.81(a), 21 CFR 807.85(a) explicitly provides that a custom device is exempt from the premarket notification requirements of 21 CFR Part 807 Subpart E if the device is within the meaning of section 520(b) of the FD&C Act, and:
  (1) It is intended for use by a patient named in the order of the physician or dentist (or other specially qualified person); OR
  (2) It is intended solely for use by a physician or dentist (or other specially qualified person) and is not generally available to, or generally used by, other physicians or dentists (or other specially qualified persons).
- Statutory Alignment (FD&C Act Section 520(b); FDA Custom Device Exemption Program Reference, https://www.fda.gov/media/89996/download, fetched 2026-11-22T23:52:49Z): A device within the meaning of section 520(b) necessarily deviates from premarket requirements because it is sufficiently unique that clinical investigations would be impractical and could not be performed to demonstrate conformance to applicable performance standards or support premarket review; it is made upon the written request of a physician or dentist to treat a unique pathology/physiological condition (patient-centric) or meet a special practice need (physician-centric), is not generally available in the United States in finished form, and orders are not solicited by the firm. Personalized or patient-fitted devices (devices legally marketed in a form modified prior to use in each patient, such as a milled dental abutment blank or patient-fitted 3D-printed orthopedic device where a conventional device is cleared) are NOT custom devices and do not qualify for this exemption.

4. Continuing Regulatory Obligations (Non-Exempt Requirements)
Although exempt from 90-day premarket notification under 21 CFR 807.85(a) and from performance standards and premarket approval (sections 514 and 515 of the FD&C Act), a custom device remains subject to applicable post-market and general controls per FDA's Custom Device Exemption Program requirements (https://www.fda.gov/media/89996/download):
- Quality System Regulation: 21 CFR Part 820 (custom devices are not exempt).
- Establishment Registration and Device Listing: 21 CFR Part 807 (registration and listing requirements still apply).
- Labeling: 21 CFR Part 801 (must provide adequate directions for use and must not be false or misleading).
- Medical Device Reporting (Adverse Event Reporting): 21 CFR Part 803.
- Corrections and Removals: 21 CFR Part 806.
- Custom Device Justification Documentation / Reporting: Documentation supporting patient-centric or physician-centric custom-device status, including device description, manufacturing/assembly details, justification of deviation from premarket requirements, statement of non-general availability, and patient/physician identifiers or special practice need statements.

5. Citations (Full Source Versions)
- 21 CFR Part 807, Subpart E (§ 807.81, as amended at 89 FR 18792, Mar. 15, 2024; § 807.85, as amended at 81 FR 70340, Oct. 12, 2016), eCFR Title 21, Chapter I, Subchapter H, Part 807, Subpart E (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-H/part-807/subpart-E; https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/part-807/section-807.85; https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-H/part-807/subpart-E/section-807.81; fetched 2026-11-22T23:52:49Z).
- 21 CFR Part 807, Subpart E, Title 21, Volume 8, 2025 Code of Federal Regulations (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title21-vol8/pdf/CFR-2025-title21-vol8-part807-subpartE.pdf; fetched 2026-11-22T23:52:49Z).
- Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, Section 520(b), as summarized in U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), Custom Device Exemption Program Presentation (https://www.fda.gov/media/89996/download; fetched 2026-11-22T23:52:49Z).

quotes.whole:
TB blood tests (Interferon Gamma Release Assay [IGRA])
TB blood tests (sometimes called IGRAs) measure the immune response in whole blood after it has been mixed with controls and with synthetic peptides that are designed to simulate TB antigens. The white blood cells in most people who have TB infection are sensitive to the test antigens and release interferon-gamma (IFN-γ). The tests measure the amount of the IFN-γ response.
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved these two TB blood tests that are commercially available in the United States:
QuantiFERON®-TB Gold Plus (QFT-Plus)
T-SPOT®.TB test (T-Spot)
Only one visit is required to draw blood for the test. TB blood tests are the preferred method of TB testing for people 5 years of age and older who have received the bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine.

Interpreting test results
Interpreting TB blood test results
Interpretation of TB blood test results depends on the test being used.
QFT-Plus results are based on the amount of IFN-γ that is released in response to the antigens and to the control substances after the blood has been incubated these substances.
T-Spot results are based on comparing the number of IFN-γ producing cells (spots) produced after the blood has been incubated with these substances.
Laboratories should provide both the qualitative and quantitative results.
For qualitative results
QFT-Plus results are reported as positive, negative, or indeterminate.

A medical evaluation for TB disease includes:
Medical history
Physical examination
Test for TB infection (TB blood test or TB skin test)
Chest x-ray
Laboratory tests to see if TB germs are present (sputum smear and culture)
Laboratory tests for drug resistance
Testing for TB infection
There are two types of tests for TB infection: the TB blood test and the TB skin test.
Current CDC guidelines recommend the TB skin test as the method of testing for children younger than 5 years of age, while noting that some experts use TB blood tests in younger children. Health care providers may choose to consult the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) guidance on the use of TB blood tests in children.
TB Blood Test
TB blood tests (also called interferon-gamma release assays or IGRAs) use a blood sample to find out if someone is infected with TB germs. The tests measure how the immune system reacts when a small amount of blood is mixed with TB proteins.
If a child is 5 years of age or older and has ever received a vaccine for TB, their health care provider should recommend the TB blood test. Unlike the TB skin test, TB blood tests are not affected by the TB vaccine (BCG vaccine).

quotes.text:
Vaccines
Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) is a vaccine for TB disease. The vaccine is not generally used in the United States. It is given to infants and small children in countries where TB is common. It protects children from getting severe forms of active TB disease, such as TB meningitis (TB disease of the brain).
The vaccine can cause a false positive TB skin test reaction. TB blood tests are the preferred tests for people 5 years of age and older who have received the BCG TB vaccine. Tell your child's health care provider if they have received the BCG TB vaccine.

Key points
The TB skin test (also known as the Mantoux tuberculin skin test or TST) is one method of determining whether a person is infected with TB bacteria.

quotes.whole:
Most people can receive a TB skin test. TB skin tests are contraindicated only for people who have had a severe reaction (e.g. necrosis, blistering, anaphylactic shock, or ulcerations to a previous TB skin test). TB skin tests are not contraindicated for any other persons, including infants, children, pregnant women, or people with HIV.
TB skin tests should not be performed on people who have written documentation of a previous positive TB test result (TB blood test or TB skin test) or treatment for TB disease. Most people who have a positive TB test result will continue to have a positive test result. Additional TB skin tests will probably not contribute to medical care, regardless of the result.
Health care providers should take into account the following factors when considering the TB skin test for a patient:
Age
Current CDC guidelines recommend the TB skin test as the method of testing for children younger than 5 years of age, while noting that some experts use TB blood tests in younger children. Health care providers may choose to consult the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) guidance on the use of TB blood tests in children.

Multiple BCG doses (as practiced in some countries) increases a person's sensitivity to the TB skin test and the duration of positive TB skin test results after BCG administration.

quotes.whole:
Health care providers treating children who have been vaccinated with BCG should also know that tuberculin reactivity is likely during the first two years after BCG administration to the newborn.
Multiple BCG doses (as practiced in some countries) increases a person's sensitivity to the TB skin test and the duration of positive TB skin test results after BCG administration.
BCG vaccination does not induce positive results when TB blood tests are used. TB blood tests are the preferred test for people who have received the BCG vaccine, including children.
Boosted reactions and two-step testing
A boosted reaction can occur in previously infected, older adults whose sensitivity to tuberculin has decreased over time. It also can occur in persons of any age who have been vaccinated with BCG or infected with mycobacteria besides M. tuberculosis complex. When given a TB skin test years after infection, these persons may have little or no reaction, giving a negative skin test result. However, the TB skin test may stimulate the immune system, causing a boosted reaction with a positive result after subsequent tests. The TB blood test does not boost subsequent test results.

Conducting a medical evaluation
Health care providers should conduct a medical evaluation for TB disease for all children who have:
A positive test result for TB infection (TB blood test or TB skin test),
Symptoms of TB disease, or
Exposure to a person with TB disease.
A medical evaluation for TB disease includes:
Medical history
Physical examination
Test for TB infection (TB blood test or TB skin test)
Chest x-ray

quotes.whole:
3. TB blood tests or TB skin test
There are two tests that are used to determine if a person has been infected with TB bacteria:
TB blood test (Interferon Gamma Release Assay [IGRA])
TB skin test (Mantoux tuberculin skin test [TST])
Selecting a test
Health care providers may consider the reasons and context for testing, test availability, and the overall cost effectiveness of testing when selecting a suitable test for TB infection.
Health care providers are encouraged to use TB blood tests to detect TB infection. TB blood tests are preferred for:
People who have received the BCG vaccine and
People who might be less likely to return for TB skin test reading and interpretation.
TB skin tests are an acceptable alternative in situations where a TB blood test is not available, is too costly, or is too burdensome.
Current CDC guidelines recommend the TB skin test as the method of testing for children younger than 5 years of age.
Interpreting test results
A positive TB blood test result or TB skin test result usually means TB infection. More tests, such as a chest radiograph, are needed to rule out TB disease.

verdict.summary:
DRAFT FOR QUALIFIED CLINICIAN REVIEW ONLY — NOT MEDICAL ADVICE AND NOT FOR DIRECT PATIENT CARE.

1. VERDICT
No. On the CDC "Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Tuberculosis" page (dated April 17, 2025; fetched 2026-11-22T23:55:19Z as representative of the page available on 2026-11-21), the stated preference for TB blood tests (interferon-gamma release assays [IGRAs]) over the TB skin test (Mantoux tuberculin skin test [TST]) does NOT apply to a 4-year-old child who previously received the bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine.

2. POPULATION, EXPOSURE, AND TESTING SCOPE
- Population: A child aged 4 years (younger than the 5-year threshold) who has received the BCG vaccine and requires testing for Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection.
- Exposure / Interventions Evaluated: Prior BCG vaccination (dose, age at administration, and number of doses unspecified) and comparison of FDA-approved TB blood tests (QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus [QFT-Plus] and T-SPOT.TB) versus the Mantoux tuberculin skin test (TST).
- Testing Context: Unspecified in the request (e.g., risk-based screening, contact investigation after exposure to active TB disease, or evaluation for symptomatic TB disease).

3. PRIMARY EVIDENCE FROM THE TARGET CDC PAGE
On CDC's "Clinical Testing and Diagnosis for Tuberculosis" page (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, updated April 17, 2025; https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/index.html; fetched 2026-11-22T23:55:19Z, sha256 9095c1db7f3e), the guidance states verbatim:
- Age-restricted BCG preference: "TB blood tests are the preferred method of TB testing for people 5 years of age and older who have received the bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine."
- Recommendation for children under 5 years of age: "Current CDC guidelines recommend the TB skin test as the method of testing for children younger than 5 years of age, while noting that some experts use TB blood tests in younger children. Health care providers may choose to consult the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) guidance1 on the use of TB blood tests in children."
- Risk-based testing constraint: "CDC recommends testing people who are at increased risk for TB infection" and "discourages a testing approach that is independent of a risk assessment."
- Operational note on IGRAs: Only 1 visit is required to draw blood for an IGRA.

Because the child is 4 years of age (less than 5 years of age), the child does not meet the age criterion (>= 5 years) attached to the TB blood test preference on this page; instead, the page's primary CDC guideline recommendation for this age group is the TB skin test (TST), while acknowledging that some experts use TB blood tests in younger children and directing clinicians to AAP guidance.

4. CORROBORATING AND CONFLICTING LANGUAGE ACROSS RELATED CDC PAGES
While the target page is unambiguous, wording across related CDC TB pages fetched on 2026-11-22T23:55:19Z shows inconsistency in how the 5-year age qualifier is stated alongside BCG status:

A. Pages consistent with the >= 5 years qualifier for BCG-vaccinated children:
1. CDC, "Tuberculosis Clinical Care for Children" (April 17, 2025; https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/clinical-care/children.html; fetched 2026-11-22T23:55:19Z, sha256 171f6557d84e): States that "Health care providers should recommend the TB blood test if a child: Is five years of age or older and Has ever received the BCG vaccine (TB vaccine)." It further notes that BCG may cause a false-positive TST reaction with no reliable way to distinguish BCG reactivity from true TB infection, and that "Interpretation of the TB skin test reaction is the same for people who have had BCG vaccination as it is for those who have not."
2. CDC, "Tuberculosis in Children" (https://www.cdc.gov/tb/about/children.html; fetched 2026-11-22T23:55:19Z, sha256 de6543e1f048): States "TB blood tests are the preferred tests for people 5 years of age and older who have received the BCG TB vaccine" and "Current CDC guidelines recommend the TB skin test as the method of testing for children younger than 5 years of age, while noting that some experts use TB blood tests in younger children."

B. Pages with unqualified BCG preference statements creating potential ambiguity:
1. CDC, "Clinical Testing Guidance for Tuberculosis: Tuberculin Skin Test" (January 31, 2025; https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/tuberculin-skin-test.html; fetched 2026-11-22T23:55:19Z, sha256 4aa43e3065d3): Under "Age," it states "Current CDC guidelines recommend the TB skin test as the method of testing for children younger than 5 years of age, while noting that some experts use TB blood tests in younger children." However, under "Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) TB vaccine," it states without an age qualifier: "TB blood tests are the preferred test for people who have received the BCG vaccine, including children." It also notes that tuberculin reactivity is likely during the first 2 years after newborn BCG administration and that multiple BCG doses increase TST sensitivity and duration of positivity.
2. CDC, "Clinical Testing Guidance for Tuberculosis: Interferon Gamma Release Assay" (May 9, 2024; https://www.cdc.gov/tb/hcp/testing-diagnosis/interferon-gamma-release-assay.html; fetched 2026-11-22T23:55:19Z, sha256 4791076e7908): Lists "People who have received the BCG vaccine" without an age qualifier under preferred IGRA populations, but immediately follows under "Age" with: "Current CDC guidelines recommend the TB skin test as the method of testing for children younger than 5 years of age, while noting that some experts use TB blood tests in younger children," noting that collecting a sufficient blood sample can be a practical barrier in very young children. It also lists specimen processing windows of 16 hours (whole blood) and 8 to 32 hours (blood cells), turnaround times as fast as 24 hours (or several days depending on the lab), and notes that live virus vaccines (e.g., measles, mumps, rubella, oral polio, varicella, yellow fever) may interfere with TB blood test reactions.
3. 5. CLINICAL CONTEXT GAPS AND LIMITATIONS IN AVAILABLE EVIDENCE
- Verification Date vs. Fetch Timestamp: The target CDC page is dated April 17, 2025, and was retrieved on 2026-11-22T23:55:19Z; an archived snapshot specifically timestamped 2026-11-21 was not separately retrieved, though the April 17, 2025 revision date supports continuity across 2026-11-21.
- Unverified External Sources Referenced by CDC: The target CDC page cites "American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) guidance1" regarding IGRA use in children younger than 5 years of age, and mentions FDA-approved assays (QFT-Plus and T-SPOT.TB). Neither the AAP guidance text nor the assay-specific FDA prescribing information/pediatric age labels were included in the fetched CDC sources and must be consulted directly by the reviewing clinician before selecting an IGRA in a 4-year-old.
- Missing Patient-Specific Clinical Details:

Indication for testing and exposure history: Per CDC's "Tuberculosis Clinical Care for Children" (April 17, 2025), children younger than 5 years of age who have spent time with an adult with TB disease require window prophylaxis (treatment for latent TB infection) even if the initial TB blood test or TB skin test is negative and fewer than 8 to 10 weeks have passed since the last exposure, and children with a positive test, symptoms, or TB exposure require a full medical evaluation including chest radiograph.
  2. Prior positive test or TB treatment: Per CDC's TST and IGRA pages, neither test should be performed if the child has written documentation of a previous positive TB test or prior TB disease treatment.

TB blood tests (Interferon Gamma Release Assay [IGRA])
TB blood tests (sometimes called IGRAs) measure the immune response in whole blood after it has been mixed with controls and with synthetic peptides that are designed to simulate TB antigens. The white blood cells in most people who have TB infection are sensitive to the test antigens and release interferon-gamma (IFN-γ). The tests measure the amount of the IFN-γ response.

CDC recommends testing people who are at increased risk for TB infection.

Children with inactive TB are infected with TB germs, but they do not have active TB disease.
Once infected with TB germs, children, especially children younger than 5 years of age, are more likely to get sick with active TB disease and to get sick more quickly than adults.
Children also have a higher risk for TB if they: Live with family members or other adults who have risk factors for TB

This guideline covers identifying and treating primary hypertension (high blood pressure) in people aged 18 and over, including people with type 2 diabetes. August 2019: We have reviewed the evidence and made new recommendations on diagnosis, monitoring and drug treatment for hypertension, and identifying who to refer for same-day specialist review. These recommendations are marked [2019].
We have also made some changes without an evidence review:
the information on cuff size for measuring blood pressure was moved to avoid repetition
plasma glucose testing was replaced with glycated haemoglobin (HbA1C) to reflect current practice
a note was added because of concerns about the risks of salt substitutes in some groups
the information on when to refer to the hypertension in pregnancy guideline was made clearer.

verdict.summary:
DRAFT FOR QUALIFIED CLINICIAN REVIEW ONLY — NOT MEDICAL ADVICE AND NOT FOR DIRECT PATIENT CARE.

1. Executive Answers
- Current NICE guideline covering the scope (Ask 1): NICE guideline NG136 (Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management; published 28 August 2019; last updated and last reviewed 26 February 2026, with a minor amendment logged October 2026 in the update history).
- Earlier NICE hypertension guideline updated and replaced (Ask 2): NICE guideline CG127.
- Additional supersession for type 2 diabetes: NG136 also updates and replaces the section on diagnosing and managing hypertension (section 1.4 / section 1.44 blood pressure management) previously contained in NICE guideline NG28 (Type 2 diabetes in adults: management; published 02 December 2015; last updated 18 February 2026; last reviewed 05 November 2026).

2. Scope, Population, and Supersession Lineage
- Population and exposure/intervention scope: Per NG136 (Overview and Recommendations), the guideline covers identifying and treating primary hypertension (measuring blood pressure, diagnosing hypertension, assessing cardiovascular risk and target organ damage, lifestyle interventions, starting antihypertensive drug treatment, monitoring treatment and blood pressure targets, and choosing antihypertensive drug treatment steps 1 to 4) in adults aged 18 years and over (population: >=18 years), explicitly including adults with type 2 diabetes.
- Direct replacement statement (NG136 Overview): "This guideline updates and replaces NICE guideline CG127. It also updates and replaces the section on blood pressure management in the NICE guideline on type 2 diabetes in adults (NG28)."
- Corroboration in NG28 (Section 1.44 and Update Information, August 2019 entry): Recommendations on diagnosing and managing hypertension were removed from NG28 and cross-referenced to NG136 because diagnosis, treatment, and monitoring of hypertension are broadly the same for adults aged 18 years and over with type 2 diabetes as for other adults, with diabetes-specific variations detailed within NG136 (for example: annual blood pressure measurement in adults with type 2 diabetes without previously diagnosed hypertension or renal disease [Rec 1.2.12]; checking for postural hypotension in adults with hypertension and type 2 diabetes [Rec 1.4.16]; and reviewing existing antihypertensive drug treatment when type 2 diabetes is diagnosed [Rec 1.4.25]).
- Note on drug doses/exposures: No specific pharmacological agent doses are evaluated in this guideline-identification summary; any pathway section covering antihypertensive steps 1 to 4 must specify drug, dose, and units per NG136 and relevant product labels.

3. Key Quantitative Thresholds and Scope Boundaries in NG136 (Cited with Population and Units)
- Clinic blood pressure targets (NG136 Tables 1 and 2):
  * Adults aged under 80 years with hypertension (with or without type 2 diabetes): target below 140/90 mmHg (Rec 1.4.20).
  * Adults aged 80 years and over with hypertension (with or without type 2 diabetes): target below 150/90 mmHg (Rec 1.4.21).
  * Note on units in Tables 1 and 2: Numeric targets (140/90 and 150/90) are stated in mmHg (consistent with standard clinic blood pressure units and NG136 Rec 1.5.1 threshold of 180/120 mmHg or more for same-day specialist referral assessment when no target organ damage is present).
- Cross-guideline boundaries where treatment differs (NG136 Recommendations, Table 1, and Update Information):
  * Chronic kidney disease (CKD) or type 1 diabetes with albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) less than 70 mg/mmol in adults aged under 80 years: clinic target below 140/90 mmHg (per NICE guidelines on CKD [Rec 1.6.1] and type 1 diabetes in adults [Rec 1.13.8]).
  * CKD or type 1 diabetes with ACR of 70 mg/mmol or more in adults aged under 80 years: clinic target below 130/80 mmHg (per NICE guidelines on CKD [Rec 1.6.2] and type 1 diabetes in adults [Rec 1.13.8]).
  * Hypertension in pregnancy and secondary causes of hypertension (Rec 1.2.13): Pathway must signpost to NICE's guideline on hypertension in pregnancy and specialist investigations where clinically indicated.

4. Guideline Currency, Evidence Gaps, and Documentation Nuances
- Currency and ongoing surveillance: NG136 states "Published: 28 August 2019" and "Last updated: 26 February 2026" (adding Rec 1.2.11 on healthy living advice for people with raised blood pressure not diagnosed with hypertension). Notably, the Update Information page also records an "October 2026" minor amendment to Rec 1.4.26 clarifying when to apply NG136 versus the CKD guideline, even though the page header still displays 26 February 2026; pathway authors should verify the latest PDF/web release date at final sign-off.
- Thin or evolving evidence flagged by NICE: NG136 explicitly notes that evidence is currently under monitoring regarding differential responses to antihypertensive drugs across ethnic groups and states NICE will decide whether to update recommendations once ongoing research is published. Additionally, NG136 notes an absence of comparative evidence identifying which single treatment is most effective at treatment step 2 or step 3, recommending an individualised choice informed by risks, benefits, and patient preference.
- Historical recommendations retained without recent review: Several NG136 recommendations inherited from earlier guidance (including Rec 1.2.12 and Rec 1.4.25 from 2009 in NG28/CG87, and Rec 1.4.24 from 2004) have not undergone a new evidence review in 2019-2026 and carry their original evidence-review year tags.

5. Full Citations
- National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE). Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management. NICE guideline [NG136]. Published: 28 August 2019; Last updated: 26 February 2026 (with October 2026 minor amendment noted in update history). Available at: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136 (Overview, Recommendations, and Update information chapters, accessed 22 November 2026).
- National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE). Type 2 diabetes in adults: management. NICE guideline [NG28]. Published: 02 December 2015; Last updated: 18 February 2026; Last reviewed: 05 November 2026. Available at: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/NG28 and PDF resource https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng28/resources/type-2-diabetes-in-adults-management-pdf-1837338615493 (accessed 22 November 2026).

quotes.whole:
§ 50.55 Requirements for permission by parents or guardians and for assent by children.




(a) In addition to the determinations required under other applicable sections of this subpart D, the IRB must determine that adequate provisions are made for soliciting the assent of the children when in the judgment of the IRB the children are capable of providing assent.






(b) In determining whether children are capable of providing assent, the IRB must take into account the ages, maturity, and psychological state of the children involved. This judgment may be made for all children to be involved in clinical investigations under a particular protocol, or for each child, as the IRB deems appropriate.






(c) The assent of the children is not a necessary condition for proceeding with the clinical investigation if the IRB determines:




(1) That the capability of some or all of the children is so limited that they cannot reasonably be consulted, or






(2) That the intervention or procedure involved in the clinical investigation holds out a prospect of direct benefit that is important to the health or well-being of the children and is available only in the context of the clinical investigation.








(d) Even where the IRB determines that the subjects are capable of assenting, the IRB may still waive the assent requirement if it finds and documents that:




(1) The clinical investigation involves no more than minimal risk to the subjects;






(2) The waiver will not adversely affect the rights and welfare of the subjects;






(3) The clinical investigation could not practicably be carried out without the waiver; and






(4) Whenever appropriate, the subjects will be provided with additional pertinent information after participation.








(e) In addition to the determinations required under other applicable sections of this subpart D, the IRB must determine, in accordance with and to the extent that consent is required under part 50, that the permission of each child's parents or guardian is granted.




(1) Where parental permission is to be obtained, the IRB may find that the permission of one parent is sufficient for clinical investigations to be conducted under § 50.51 or § 50.52.






(2) Where clinical investigations are covered by § 50.53 or § 50.54 and permission is to be obtained from parents, both parents must give their permission unless one parent is deceased, unknown, incompetent, or not reasonably available, or when only one parent has legal responsibility for the care and custody of the child.








(f) Permission by parents or guardians must be documented in accordance with and to the extent required by § 50.27.





(g) When the IRB determines that assent is required, it must also determine whether and how assent must be documented.



[66 FR 20598, Apr. 24, 2001, as amended at 78 FR 12951, Feb. 26, 2013]

verdict.summary:
DRAFT REGULATORY ANALYSIS FOR QUALIFIED CLINICIAN REVIEW — NOT MEDICAL OR LEGAL ADVICE AND NOT FOR PATIENT CARE.

1. Scope, Population, and Exposure
- Population: Human subjects eligible for enrollment in an FDA-regulated clinical investigation as defined in 21 CFR § 50.3(c) (eCFR Title 21, Part 50, accessed 2026-11-23), including general adult populations, children as defined in 21 CFR § 50.3 and governed by 21 CFR Part 50 Subpart D (66 FR 20598, Apr. 24, 2001, as amended at 78 FR 12951, Feb. 26, 2013), and subjects in life-threatening emergencies governed by 21 CFR § 50.24.
- Dose or Exposure: Not applicable to a specific investigational product; this regulatory assessment applies generically to any experiment involving an FDA-regulated test article and 1 or more human subjects subject to prior submission under section 505(i) or 520(g) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act or intended for submission to/inspection by FDA (21 CFR § 50.3(c)).
- Regulatory Baseline Date: 21 CFR Part 50 as in force on 2026-11-21 (verified against eCFR current text fetched 2026-11-23).

2. Verdict (Ask 2): Is Minimal Risk Alone Sufficient to Enroll Without Informed Consent?
No. Under 21 CFR Part 50 as in force on 2026-11-21, the fact that a clinical investigation involves no more than minimal risk is NOT sufficient on its own for an investigator to enroll a person without informed consent.

First, an investigator cannot unilaterally waive informed consent; only the responsible Institutional Review Board (IRB) may approve a consent waiver or alteration after making and documenting specific regulatory findings (21 CFR § 50.22; 88 FR 88248, Dec. 21, 2023).

Second, under 21 CFR § 50.22 ("Exception from informed consent requirements for minimal risk clinical investigations," 88 FR 88248, Dec. 21, 2023), minimal risk is only 1 of 5 required criteria (4 criteria if identifiable private information or identifiable biospecimens are not used). Specifically, the IRB responsible for the review, approval, and continuing review of the clinical investigation may approve an informed consent procedure that omits or alters some or all elements of informed consent in 21 CFR § 50.25(a) and (b), or waive the requirement to obtain informed consent, only if the IRB finds and documents ALL of the following:
- (a) Minimal Risk: "The clinical investigation involves no more than minimal risk to the subjects" (21 CFR § 50.22(a));
- (b) Impracticability of Research: "The clinical investigation could not practicably be carried out without the requested waiver or alteration" (21 CFR § 50.22(b));
- (c) Impracticability Regarding Identifiable Data/Biospecimens: "If the clinical investigation involves using identifiable private information or identifiable biospecimens, the clinical investigation could not practicably be carried out without using such information or biospecimens in an identifiable format" (21 CFR § 50.22(c));
- (d) Rights and Welfare: "The waiver or alteration will not adversely affect the rights and welfare of the subjects" (21 CFR § 50.22(d)); and
- (e) Post-Participation Information: "Whenever appropriate, the subjects or legally authorized representatives will be provided with additional pertinent information after participation" (21 CFR § 50.22(e)).

Third, additional or distinct requirements apply to special populations and contexts:
- Children (21 CFR Part 50, Subpart D): Children are persons who have not attained the legal age for consent to treatments or procedures involved in clinical investigations under applicable local law (21 CFR § 50.3). Under 21 CFR § 50.51 (78 FR 12951, Feb. 26, 2013), a clinical investigation presenting no greater than minimal risk to children may involve children only if the IRB finds both that no greater than minimal risk is presented (§ 50.51(a)) and that adequate provisions are made for soliciting child assent and parental/guardian permission as set forth in § 50.55 (§ 50.51(b)). Parental/guardian permission is required in accordance with and to the extent that consent is required under Part 50 (§ 50.55(e)), with permission of 1 parent sufficient for investigations under § 50.51 or § 50.52 (§ 50.55(e)(1)) and 2 parents required under § 50.53 or § 50.54 unless an exception in § 50.55(e)(2) applies. Even for waiving child assent alone (when children are capable of assenting), the IRB must find and document 4 criteria under 21 CFR § 50.55(d)(1)–(4): minimal risk, no adverse effect on rights and welfare, impracticability without the waiver, and post-participation information whenever appropriate.
- Emergency Research (21 CFR § 50.24): The Part 50 emergency research exception from informed consent is not triggered by minimal risk; instead, it requires a life-threatening situation with unproven or unsatisfactory available treatments, infeasibility of consent, prospect of direct benefit, impracticability without the waiver, concurrence of a non-participating licensed physician IRB member/consultant, submission under a separate IND or IDE (§ 50.24(d)), post-enrollment notification procedures, and IRB record retention for at least 3 years after completion of the clinical investigation (§ 50.24(c)).

3. Definition of Minimal Risk (Ask 3): How Does 21 CFR Part 50 Define Minimal Risk?
21 CFR § 50.3(k) (eCFR Title 21, Part 50, § 50.3, fetched 2026-11-23) defines minimal risk verbatim as:
"Minimal risk means that the probability and magnitude of harm or discomfort anticipated in the research are not greater in and of themselves than those ordinarily encountered in daily life or during the performance of routine physical or psychological examinations or tests."

4. Operational Guidance for Clinical Research Application
If an investigator wishes to enroll subjects without informed consent in a minimal-risk FDA-regulated clinical investigation, the research team must submit a written justification to the responsible IRB demonstrating each applicable criterion in 21 CFR § 50.22(a)–(e) (and 21 CFR Part 50 Subpart D if children are enrolled), rather than relying on minimal risk status alone, and must not enroll any subject without prior IRB approval and documentation of those findings.

- U.S. Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR § 50.22 (Exception from informed consent requirements for minimal risk clinical investigations), 88 FR 88248, Dec. 21, 2023, Electronic Code of Federal Regulations (eCFR), https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/part-50/section-50.22 (fetched 2026-11-23T00:02:28Z).
